A bowling alley was not what Jack expected. Only a moment ago he'd been sitting in the middle of the road, fighting for air and in incredible pain. The next thing he knew he was standing at the shoe rental counter, staring into the face of a lumpy-faced old guy. "Where am I?" Lumpy-face grunted eloquently before speaking, "You're dead, kid. This is your afterlife." Jack took another look around, spotting too many fashions from the seventies and not enough young women, "Here?" "Yup." "What is this?" "The Final Lane; the hereafter for all who followed the tenants of Dudeism, Man." An older guy came up behind Jack and put an arm around his shoulder. "Jeff Bridges?" Jack stared at the man beside him, "The hell?" "Relax, man." Jeff guided Jack from the counter and over to a table with a pitcher of beer on it, "Just chill out." "But..." Jack stammered, "I'm dead!" "Yup." Bridges nodded, "Happens to all of us." "Aren't I supposed to go to heaven..... or hell, or something?" "Sit down." Jeff flopped down in his own chair and Jack followed suit, settling himself into the hard and ancient plastic, "Jack, it's like this. This afterlife shit, it's not like they tell you back on earth. You don't go where people tell you you'll go, you go where you'll fit in, right? Whatever cosmic shit that weighs us and shit said, like,'Hey, this dude's Ok. He can go hang with the Lebowski." "Lebowski?" "Oh, yeah man." Jeff waved lazily at the world around him, "This is all, like, some movie shit. Buncha dudes turned it into a religion. Basically, they made a belief system based around just chilling out. Yeah? You're were probably pretty laid back in life, let everybody just do their own thing without getting all pissy about it, am I right?" Jack thought about his life and found he couldn't really argue with scruffy Jeff Bridges. "So this is it?" "Nah, man." Bridges took a drink, "There's a bar as well, and a parking lot." "This sucks." "That's just, like, your opinion, man."

Brian Lindale cursed at his wife's dogs, like he did every day. Except this time, when he told the purebred Yorkshire terrier to "Die like the rat you are," he meant it. He could deal with the smell they built up over spending hours in their kennels, or the 2am barking that would spark the others to echo that sharp yipping. He even managed to somehow forgive when the smallest one chewed through the power cables on his 66" flat screen television, right when he really needed to just sit and watch something distracting for an hour. But now, images of drowning the animals in their swimming pool were tempted to stay in his mind's eye. Hell, he'd even bury them afterwards, which would be more then they deserve. He hated them especially today because now instead of leaving the house five minutes early, he would be leaving just on time. He checked the clock on his phone. 7:00. Takes twenty minutes to get there, interviews at 7:30. I'll be fine he hoped. Brian carried their kennels to the back door and opened their little gates. He gagged at the smell, and realizing that there was shit even on the handles. He rushed to the kitchen sink to wash his hands immediately, using too much dish soap as he always did. Brian was the type of person who liked clean hands, and if they were ever dirty at some point in the day, he would feel anxious. And even worse, Brian bit his nails down to the flesh, so he had to be extra careful to avoid situations like these. Scrubbing that bit of brown on his hand that just wouldn't come off, he looked up to find the dogs playing with each other, covering their white fur with shit and piss. He looked over to his phone. It showed only a black screen. Brian nudged the front button with his elbow and it showed 7:03. Ill be fine He stepped over the kennels to get to the backyard, careful not to swing the door open too much so the little rats couldn't scurry inside. He scolded them as they tried to jump on his legs. "Shoo, you little shits. Get the fuck away from me." He managed to get to the side of the house, walking barefoot over their white rock landscaping, peppered with bits of dry dog shit. He evaded them all and got to the green hose the gardeners used to water their four palm trees. He traced the hose to its source and turned the spout. He held the hose up, and chilling cold water dribbled out from the tip. He held his thumb on it, but there wasn't enough pressure to make a spray. Brian had to trace the hose again to find where it had folded, and found it on the third try. The pressure inside the hose finally let out, spraying water straight into the air. Now he had dirty water on him, but he didn't care. After this, he would need to shower again anyway. He held his thumb to the tip and sprayed the hose water at the dogs. Of course, they took him for playing and tried to jump at him. If his wife saw him repelling the little rats now by spraying directly into their faces, she would be livid. They misbehave because they know you hate them! she would say. It was the kind of thing that he thought was cute when she said it, but thinking on it later would just irritate him. What kind of sense does that make? Shitting on yourself must be some protest When finally they were as white as their innocent little souls, Brian ushered them into their spare kennels. Of course, the last one never wanted to go back in once he had been let out. But like Brian, we don't all get what we want. He carried their now full kennels inside, trying not to let their yipping get on his nerves. He set them down, walked back to the kitchen sink and checked his phone. 7:08. I'll be fine The shower was nice, at least. He liked his showers hot enough to fog the mirrors. But he didn't have the time to stew in it long. He jumped out, toweled off and slipped into his extra suit. As he walked out the door, he checked his phone. 7:15 If I hurry, I'l be fine Brian powered on his GPS device, and waited anxiously for his directions. Suddenly the screen went dark. Dead? No not now He pressed the power button desperately, but nothing else happened. "Damn NSA" he said aloud. The National Security Agency years ago made a deal with global phone providers to record all audio around every cellular device, and to shut down phones before all power was depleted in order to maintain recording. At least, that's what he had heard. He cursed the NSA out of habit, but also to try and make light of this awful situation. Brian certainly remembered where he was going: for a job interview at the local paper to write a sports column. The press factory for the Reno Times was the largest building in town, outside of North Virgiinia Street. Damn near every schoolboy in the city worked as their paperboys back in the 60s, when he grew up. Times were simpler then. Dogs stayed outside, phones didn't die and employers understood if you had a bad morning coming in. But now, companies just dont care. With one of every seven people unemployed, the companies could be as hard as they wanted on their workers. What would they do, quit? Good luck feeding your family. It was a kind of leverage that would be called criminal, back when Brian grew up. Now it's just good business. He checked his phone again to check the time. Still dead. No idea how late I am Nervously he looked at his hand, and found the nail on his right pinky finger just a bit longer than the others, showing the tiniest sliver of white at the tip. He bit down, remembered his cleaning work that morning, and gagged. He spat outside his window. Best not to think about it. Think about the road, we got ta hurry on Brian backed out of the driveway and went. The kids were on summer break, so there wouldn't be any pedestrians running about trying to catch busses or chase playballs. He remembered almost hitting a child while he was checking his phone for the time. He remembered the panic, a kind of trance you enter where everything can go wrong and your mouth tastes like metal. But seeing no pedestrians around, he sped out of his home. While driving, you always believe you're hitting every red light. Like a man in a traffic control tower is looking at you, making sure the yellow light comes on just far enough away to make you doubt yourself. But now he was certain of it. Brian passed by Piggy Pete's Coffee, which was really just a donut shop with week old coffee. This was the type of place that stayed open until 11pm so the city's hipsters could eat donuts snobbily, if that were a thing. He remembered being a kind of social rebel back then, insisting that his friends listen to the Stones instead of the Beatles, and before that Beatles instead of Elvis. But only the young have time for that now, and certainly not Brian. Traffic slowed to a crawl, and Brian cursed aloud. "Are you fucking kidding me, what now?" He nudged his car to the right so he could look ahead. A quarter mile ahead, on the side of the road, a red minivan had sideswiped a green honda. It was always the green hondas. It's like people who can't drive gravitate to cheap cars they can use up and throw away. But what bothered Brian was that everyone wanted to slow and see what was going on. He wasn't the kind to nose into other people's business, especially one so boring as a traffic accident. But sure enough, every single person driving by bneeded to slow and inspect it. And once they had, they revved up to meet the normal Reno driving speed: Speed Limit 10. When he had finally broken free of the slump, he reached that certain Reno Go, everyone in a rush to get nowhere. Except he had to rush to the Reno Times, and now he finally saw their large sign just around the I-580. Reno Times it flashed. 7:35pm he panicked. August 5th Don't Text and Drive He raised his fingernails to bite them, remembered the smell of shit, and grimaced. He looked down at his hand for a second and found it: a dab of dog dung on his wrist. Somehow he missed it while washing. Oh god, what if I went into the interview like this He looked up at the road again and found the RT Drive exit coming, where he would need to turn off. Suddenly the smell of shit was giving him immense anxiety. He would need to wash it off now. Brian turned the wheel toward the exit, and started steering the wheel with his knees. He leaned over to the glove box where he kept a small stack of napkins. He pulled one out and wiped off his wrists, looking up at the road every half second to make sure he was still in his lane.He finally wiped his wrist clean when the wheel sllipped over his knee. He quickly grabbed the wheel, napkin still in hand. "GOD FUCKING DAMN IT" He let go of the hand holding the napkin and it stuck to the steering wheel, held in place with wet dog shit. He rolled down the windows to let out the smell as he turned into the Reno Times parking lot. He came to the end of a line at parking validation, each driver waiting their turn to get a ticket. Come on, come on. Get your fucking ticket already he cursed to himself, realizing the absurdity of what he said but he didn't care. These people needed to hurry up. Now.

Long and ago and even today, an old man wanders in the outlands. We hope he stays there. He is cursed. Once, the old man was an older man. A man of family, name, and life which he could not part from. When his time came, the man wished to gamble for another day. Death brought him to the brothers to strike a bet, for Death is only one face of many. The Three Brothers decide what tales must end- of course so ones may begin. The youngest prefers the name of Misfortune. They say the First Brother arrogantly tried to have the hand of Lady Luck. She needed no suitors, and punished him with her dirty deeds. The middle calls himself by Folly or Plague, whichever his mood dictates. When life first sprung forth from the land, the Second Brother pushed it back down. The Third, the eldest, has no name. The Third is the strongest by no comparison. We have only just begun to find words to pin down part of his title. Perhaps it was he who cut the skies from the world, the order from the primeval chaos, and the one who threatens to take it back. A game of cards decided the fate of the man. He won against the Brothers easily. They let him go- it was the deal struck and Death is fair to all after-all. But, humanity never feels content with what it already has. Thrice the man stole glory from their hands, gloated into their face, and a lit their eyes. A small glass filled with water, the elixir of immortality to keep the reaper at bay for how ever long one can desire. A deck of cards to gamble with Fate to force the Brothers' hands on a different course. A sack to hold the evils of the world back. The man grew old. He wasted his ill gotten spoils. He threw the water into the face of the First Brother after a sip. None left in the glass to keep the First brother from taking his family. He played Fate's hand to many times to keep blood away from the home front. His homeland was torn into pieces and wiped from the lens of history personally by the Second Brother when the cards were too worn to play again.... He sealed away disasters which would have destroyed many souls many times over. The Third Brother smirked at the idea of his plaything stopping his goals. As man traded youth for wisdom, and saved the sack for one more day. The day when he can seal the Third and ransom for forgiveness. The old man, must wander. The First and Second Brother jeer at the old man, revenge for the same he had done to them. The Third Brother told them to do more than that. If the old man ever finds a home of his fellow man, it is torn down the Brothers. They don't care who falls with the rubble, just as long as the old man knows what he wrought. For this vagabond will never find a home. He always wanders, nothing will stop the Brothers from prodding the old man further. Should you ever gamble with Death for your life there is one thing you must never do. Win.

I guess you could say I've seen things - travelled the world and all that - and so I suppose I should be grateful that it was he who bought me, who chose me as his favourite; that he always wears such smart things for his best and most thrilling jobs, and me. I sit close against soft weaves and heavy fabrics, fancy buttons sometimes - and I'm his constant. It's mostly the same to me, though. I ride along half-nestled in silk, smooth and languid and unhurried; a room in a nice hotel, measured rise and slow fall; someone else - another man, and in a beautiful suit, usually; perhaps a start, or the beginnings of a pink mouth open to wail. Bang, bang. The patterns, when they come, are a lovely red. I'd ache for a silk with colour like that. We leave, more quickly, after. I know because I count the time. It won't be long before I'm gone again, put away with his other killing things. The times in between are long, but these days are worth it. I spend the darkness remembering the silk, the weave. Bang, bang - the colours. Bang, bang. That's my constant.

Dark, darkness darker then black. Still, my heart beats. In an instance, it has cadence, and its tempo rises. The breath become heavy, the lungs become wider. Intergalactic beams penetrating archaic force fields, that magnify its power. A vague sensation of heat. The heart began to relax amidst the comfort of an energetic shroud. Then the ears, they ache to a beast who cries to the sky, for it has wings, yet cant fly. Its fate, to be consumed. So as my mind suddenly find's itself conscious, after a fleeting vague struggle. I too am melancholy, to be consumed again by the day.

The colors!, John thought. So beautiful! So this is what it's like! And suddenly he got tears in his eyes. So this is what he had been missing, all those years! He had no time to analyze what was happening, his emotions where too strong. All he could think of was to touch, to paint, to bemuse this silhouette. He wanted to capture it, to consume it. But then something struck him. Other than himself, no one looked at this person. Also, the colored man had to evade other people as they passed him in the busy city center, they never seemed to get out of the way. And when he got on board the tram with him, so as not to let him get away, he saw that the man did not pay, just walked straight passed the tram driver and sat down on the front most seat. It was then that it appeared to him that he was the only one that could see this man. The tram rushed trough the city, leaving the neat, large stores and restaurants of the city center, for the monotonous homes of the poorer districts and finally the forlorn sheds and decaying factories that made up the outskirts. The vibrantly colored man in the front seat sat unmoved, gazing out of the window, like himself. The tram rushed on, to evermore dense and poor neighborhoods, everything seemed to be made out of concrete, a bridge overhead, then a tunnel, then out in the light again. The rain lay in pools on the pavement, old newspapers and soggy cardboard got pulled up and lain down by the wind. Color. So there it had been. So beautiful as to bring tears into ones eyes. A symphony, a gift, fallen out of the sky. The tram shook. The sky was blue. Which color would that be? The beautiful dark one, the one his hat was made of? It reminded him of his mother. Could that be the color of the sky? And the light one, the one his skin was made of? Could that be the color of concrete? Would they fit together? Would nature have devised it that way, would that be artistic enough? Of course not. How could he compare with the great creator, he wasn't even an artist. But he could, he had to become one. It wasn't something he really wanted as much as a necessity, a painful thing he would now be forced to do for the rest of his life. Painting. With colors he couldn't see. With just the memory of this man as a guide. When he felt the tram shake a second time, he realized with a great shock that the man had left. He rushed towards the nearest tram doors, looking out of the window if he could see him. There he was in the distance, entering a tunnel underneath a bridge, just about to disappear round a corner. He reached the doors, bracing himself against the tram's shaking, as it got ready to move again. 'Stop!', he yelled at the driver. But it was too late. He tried if he could force the doors open, desperately yelling, 'Stop!', at the tram driver for a second time. In a fit of rage he slammed his fists against the door, then kicked it, turned around to kick it harder, ignoring the other passengers as they closed in. Then he got as far back as he could, ran up to the doors and kicked them open with his right foot, falling out of the train and rolling over the pavement, he got up as quickly as he could, not minding the intense pain in his arms and knees, not minding the blood, loosing no time to shake of the dust from his knees, not loosing time, he could still catch him, he knew it, it was destined. He ran as hard as he could, his legs feeling weak. Into the tunnel, around the corner, out trough the other side of the tunnel. It had started to rain. There he was, finally a warm flash of that beautiful color, disappearing behind a large, vacant office building. 'Sir!' he screamed. He picked up pace. He nearly had him. 'Sir!' he screamed again with the last of his voice. The man came within eye site again. 'Sir! Sir I can see you! Sir!' Then the man did something unusual. He started to climb over a small wall. John understood what was going. 'No!', he screamed and ran after him, as fast as he could. He climbed after him. Underneath him, trains came thundering by deafening the ears, with a might that was awful and unstoppable. He closed in on the patch of color, standing inches from the railroad track, leaning back and forth. 'Don't do it! I can see you! Sir! I need you!' He touched the man's shoulder. Then a train rushed by and the colored man was gone. Snatched from his sight, from right under his nose. After a few silent minutes he turned around, climbed back over the wall, trying to forget what he saw. He walked all the way home, in his hand a colored jacket.

My eyes quickly dart around the table, assessing the situation. Eight star systems, three population hubs, and two remaining opponents. Usually I don't do this well, games like this aren't really my bag of cats, but hey as long as I'm here I can be glad I'm doing well. There were six when we started, but Trillatrix's merciless and fast-moving playstyle swiftly eliminated the uncaring and unprepared. Typically I was among those when I played with her, but hey, lucky me I guess. The sly woman smirks at me from across the table, trying to read my poker face. The bitch can literally do that too, and it always makes things weird and uncomfortable. Playing with a God of Mind always is, though. " Would you take your damnable turn already, Kindred? Our little universe will collapse into entropic lead before we even get a chance to mess with it. " " Trilla, for millennia we've played this game on Tuesday nights, and every single game, you harass me about my insistence upon making wise and calculated moves. Not everyone uses overpowered crap, you know. " The other remaining opponent is, of course, Kindred, the thinly bearded outer god who played host to our functions. He's exaggerating of course, we did sometimes do other things on Tuesday nights. This game is mentally engaging and boasts a huge variety of strategic approaches and ultimate outcomes, but it was hard to take it seriously sometimes with its tendency to devolve into a patience-testing series of one-upmanship contests between players. Since the actual goal of the game is so complex and multi-faceted (and more importantly, changes every time) the temptation to just throw out stupid combinations to fuck around with everyone is incredibly hard to resist. Or, I thought to myself, you could just be like Trilla, and base your entire strategy on that very thing. " Aww, you poor, fragile thing. I play a Space-Transcending Horrorking one time and I'm still bearing with the conversational consequence. " Kindred rolled his eyes and finally played a card, causing the table's imager to change rapidly, zooming dramatically across the galaxyscape. " We don't SPEAK of that incident. We don't even THINK about it anymore, especially since even an immortal can go insane by having the audacity to comprehend that play. Guess that explains what happened to you. " She laughed and per the norm quickly slaps down a few cards, adding to his initial play. The table depicts a vast new galaxy, spinning and swirling out of nothingness, ready to foster a new set of evolutionary paths and life-bearing planetoids. Or like with most cases, a spitting contest, judging by Trilla's chemical imbalance run she's setting up. God, I hate this game sometimes. They both turn to me, obviously only half-interested. I don't have any good cards yet and I can usually only muster the most boring type of universal occurrences. The one time I actually did something cool, having my own little group of semi-advanced races working in an alliance to move their entire solar system out of the way of a giga-star about to go supernova, some asshole summoned an Eldritch Cataclysm Hydra and killed them. I sigh and put down a couple of Variety cards, the intricate circuits on the back of each one containing the billions of genetic sequences required to integrate them into the new galaxy, making it more complex, diverse. Kindred nods and checks his cards. " Good, good. I think we're just about done here. " " Really, now are we really almost done, or Kindred almost done? How many more years are we talking? " " Woman, please. " They go on like this for a few more rounds before slowly, almost unbelievably, the three of us actually have a nice little universe going. Orderly, vast, and free of reality-bending space-terrors, the entire thing was displayed on the table, infinite possibilities stretched downwards into the lacquer wooden cosmos. To some, it would be an inspiring, life-changing view. To others, it's an invitation to start screwing around. Trillatrix plays a few cards and creates a Cytoplasm Drinker to start messing with the biology on Kindred's planets. Hoping to curry her good side, I help her out with a few resources of my own, increasing the heat of a few star quadrants to make life inhospitable in most of his territory. He glares, but politely informs us he doesn't appreciate these two-on-one tactics, trying to remain candid as always. Trilla giggles and keeps experimenting with her cards, trying to make the strangest things happen, preferably to Kindred. I spend some time trying to figure out the game itself. Another aspect of this thing I hate is that the goals of the game are usually completely arbitrary and don't really have any deeper meaning behind them. Mostly everyone just does random shit until someone wins. " C'mon, play your planet corrupters, I remember you have them " I do indeed have planet corrupters, but if I keep helping her then it'll be all the worse later on. I decide to just keep building up civilization with a few industrial revolutions and progressivism movements on my largest planet. She pouts a little, and Kindred just rolls his eyes. He's practically out of the game now, nearly out of cards and exerting little influence on our universe. Suddenly, the victory screen pops up. Completely out of nowhere, with no warning. Even more disturbingly, it's in front of me. Me?! I just won? What?! The other two don't even notice at first, it's so sudden. Trillatrix's coal-black eyes widen and Kindred stares in disbelief. " That... what in the seven hells? How did you just win?! " I'm at a loss for words as I check the win conditions. Okay, set up a civilization, that's easy... create such and such lifeforms with such and such traits, yeah... and they have to... move an asteroid? I quickly drag the screen over to the exact victory point and see that, in fact, one of the civilizations developed space-flight capability, found an asteroid rich with minerals, and built a massive engine capable of moving it closer, into their planet's orbit, so that they could harvest them more easily. This simple act of ingenuity had probably taken them decades to pull off, but with this, one of the tiny little blips on the enormous game HUD would kindly inform us that this civilization has experienced an economy boost. I sit back in my chair, completely at a loss. I'd just been thinking about arbitrary winning conditions, but none of us in all our millennia of playing had seen the game do this before. Trillatrix fumes a little, her fists clenched. Kindred looks shocked, but not unamused. " Astounding, really, what can happen in this game. Truly a spectacle to behold. " She turns her glare on him, small embers appearing in her black pools for eyes. " This is complete horse-shit! I'm going to burn down the houses of the developers of this game. What a bunch of shit. " She slumps down in her chair and performs a simple card-combiner move, making a few simple cards into a more complicated one. In the manner of someone wanting to show off their hand of cards after a game is over, she slaps down the card. Immediately, the table's simulated view glows bright red. Kindred and I frown and lean over the table. It's a card we've never seen. " An interdimensional plague card... Ruby-Laced Oblivion Virus? " She smirks a little. " I just got it, and it's so cool! I couldn't wait to destroy you both with this, after I had my fun of course god, what a bullshit outcome though. I'll have to use this thing another time. " The planet the screen was zoomed in on was experiencing a serious meltdown inside its nickel-aluminum core. Already, it was on the verge of meltdown, and the actual effects were still unseen. Geez, and she was on about my planet corrupters. We all watch for the few moments it takes for the simulation to run its course. Quickly reading through the codes for the card suggests a highly complicated, extremely efficient planet-eater virus that... before I even finish reading, it's on screen, enormous firey cracks spreading across the planet's surface, its tectonic plates destabilizing. Wiry red tendrils grow from the core like colossal forests of vampiric trees, winding and tangling with themselves in their race to devour everything. And just like that, the planet's gone, obliterated along with the civilization I'd maintained for most of the game. The scarred, crimson remains of it began pulsating before exploding outwards, sending microscopic red seeds in an omnidirectional spread through the universe, towards other unsuspecting systems. Kindred just shakes his head and whistles. " Great, another overpowered card to contend with. I suppose I'll see you both next week then? " Trillatrix nods, the flames in her eyes fading a bit as she watches the carnage. They each wave their goodbyes, and I pack up my cards in the little bag I use. It kind of looks douchey, but whatever, it keeps things organized. Kindred flips off the light as we head out, plunging the room into darkness, save for the pale glow coming from the table. It isn't like it switches off.

I scribbled on my pad as I listened to my psychologist. I insisted on having something to do during our session - sitting on a couch and answering questions seemed pointless. The end result yielded nothing tangible, nothing useful, and nothing even symbolically beautiful. It was a waste of time, and I didn't have any need for that. " Just look around... " The psychologist pleaded. " There are so many people in the world. Almost seven billion different people. " " I know. " I said, as I continued to scratch on the paper. " So, how can you also believe you are the sole surviving human? " I wanted to leave this question open. I was hoping he could think hard enough and figure it out. I was hoping I wouldn't have the spell it out for him. But, alas, he wasn't human, and so he didn't understand. The psychologist sighed. " Well, our time is up today. You can pay at the front counter. " I stayed on the couch for a few moments, and finished my drawing. The doctor waited for me, tapping his foot impatiently, but he waited nonetheless. When I finished, I decided that this is the time I would answer. I stood up, holding the pad in my hand. I flipped it around for him to see - it was a drawing of his wife and son, a recreation of the picture he had displayed at the front counter. I handed it to him and told him that he could have it. He smiled, and thanked me profusely. " There are so many people, sure, so many homo sapien animals out there, but there aren't any humans left. " I told him, turning towards the door. " I live in a world that worships money and lies. I live in a world where creativity is lost among us, generosity has been destroyed. The fabric of community has fallen apart in a world where animals pretend to place meaning on sacred constructs, like marriage, only to flee once things get tough, like an animal. I go to an institution that pretends to care about me for an hour, but the reality is that there isn't any care left, there's only greed. I live in a world where we could choose to educate our people, and share our knowledge, but we insist on bombing people who don't think exactly like us, like animals. I live in a world where we could share our goods freely, and contribute to a healthy society, but we don't because too many people would take advantage of the situation, to steal or do nothing at all - like animals. I live in a world where those who have the power to do good use that power to help themselves, like animals proving they are the alpha in their pack. I live in a world where people pretend to be humans, but are actually all animals. " " But I am different. I want to help. I don't care that I spent twenty years learning to be a doctor, my time is worth the same as anyone else's, and I will heal those who need it for free, because I'm human. I don't care that I can draw, I want to share my art, because it creates smiles and warmth - this is human. I don't care how difficult a promise is to fulfill, I will keep it, because it's human. And when I see the shortcomings of people, I have realized, I am the last human." The psychologist swallowed in his chair as he slunk deeper into the fold. " So, next session in one week? " He asked meekly. I shook my head. Fucking animal.

We arrived in Fredericton, Canada at 4:35 am on June 20th, 2015 after reports of widespread rioting had reached our base - Naval Air Station Brunswick, south of the boarder in Maine. Were were the first responders. They were all dead. Everyone in the city was in a cape or a mask or spandex. It looked like Halloween met Jonestown. Many of the dead were holding each other's collars, some were in groups that appeared to have attacked and killed each other simultaneously. It was a gruesome sight to behold. As our fire team swept the city searching for threats or survivors, we came upon one middle-aged woman in a purple unitard with a mask that appeared to be made out of a doily. She was clinging to life with several crudely built and brightly painted weapons piercing her flesh. With her last few breaths she told us what had happened "I am Defender Doily. I have failed. I tried to thwart the mob of masked bandits..... but they outnumbered me..... they all claimed to be fighting for justice, but I know in my heart they were villains possessed by greed. There must have been more than 50 thousand of them. Men, women, children. They all attacked each other shouting slogans and ridiculous fake superhero names. I tried to tell them to'STOP, and BEHOLD THE INDUBITABLE DUE PROCESS OF THE DOILY DEFENDER!' But they all called me a villain and attacked me." She passed on a moment later, and I pulled the doily mask over her eyes as a last sign of respect. The fireteams scoured the rest of city, but found no other survivors. We did, however, find stapled to the Mayor's desk chair. It read: "The people of this wretched town, Hated me and tore me down; I convinced them all the rest were me, A settled score, as you can see. -Moncton Marauder"

He just had gotten into a huge fight with his wife. She threatened to take away the kids if he continued to drink. He was fed up with her and thought he should be able to do what he wants to do to himself. No one should tell him how to live his life he thought. Stumbling his way to the bar grabbing onto poles and any object he could to keep himself up. Fuck her and fuck the kids he mumbled under his breath. Bar after bar told him to get lost as he stumbled around to find a place he could get one last drink. One last drink to fuel his addiction. He stood in front of a bar with a name in a different language he did not understand or care to understand. He plopped himself down and slurred his words in a demanding tone for a tall glass of any beer they had. The bartender poured him drink and grinned his way. One sip later and he was in the mind of his children. They were crying and holding their mother. Why is daddy so mean? Mommy why is daddy never home.... Does he even love us?" A tear streamed down the mans face. He got up pushed the beer away. The bartender smirked. Do you choose death or serenity?

The restaurant was filled with men and women in clean suits and long dresses, blouses that revealed too much skin and shirts that, had they been any tighter, the buttons would have most definitely found their way across the dining hall and into the depths of a shining wine glass sitting on the many tables amongst the chattering mouths and shrieking utensils. "How's your steak?" Yusef asked his date, a beautiful red-haired woman he'd been dating for seven years. "Wonderful," she replied. "Chewy and just right. And yours?" "These lips haven't tasted meat this delicious in all my years," the fair-skinned man said with a wet smile on his sweaty face. "Say, Tori, let's play a simple game, shall we?" "Yusi, over dinner?" "This one will be simple, love. Shall we?" She nodded, taking a sip of the chardonnay. "Truth, or dare?" "Yusi, we have been together for ages now." She wiped her lips with the napkin. "What kind of game are you playing here?" "Now, now. You must choose one!" He stuffed another slice of steak into his mouth, chewing violently with a wide smile. "If I must..... I'll choose dare." Yusef swallowed the meat and threw back the entire glass of wine, pushed his chair out from the table with a quick kick of his heel, and threw the table the to side, as if possessed. A few of the guests shrieked as the table flew across the dining hall, two women fell out of their chairs and landed on their backsides, an elderly man with thick-framed glasses and fake teeth dropped his head on the table and fainted, and the neighboring diners gasped and jumped. Those who remained seated, unphased by the man's psychotic stunt, focused their attention on Yusef, who was now out of his seat, bending on one knee with a small box in his right hand. "Tori Gurid, I dare you to marry me?" Her eyes glistened wide with excitement and legs trembled underneath the tight blue dress. "Yusef! You crazy fool. I'm both embarrassed and entirely shocked." "Tori!" "I'm sorry, Yusef. Yes! Yes, I will marry you, you crazy idiot!" Those around them, those who weren't sprawled on the ground or faint over their plate of expensive cuisine, cheered and hollered. Yusef rose off his knee and leaned forward, kissing Tori on the lips. "Yusef," she asked. "Mhm?" "What would you have done had I chose the other?" "Tori, oh, Tori." He laughed. "Well for starters, I wouldn't have thrown the table!"

I fell, and as I fell, I watched the universe age. Slowly at first, then accelerating into blinding motion as I approached the event horizon slower and slower. Then the motion started to subside, as the universe began to reach heat death. I saw other supermassive black holes approaching one another, eating each other up and vanishing in bursts of Hawking radiation. I saw my event horizon shrink as well, vanishing slower than any other I had seen. As it shrank, I stopped slowing and began to fall at a constant velocity relative to the shrinking singularity. As the rest of the black holes vanished, I noticed that the universe seemed to shrink. Perhaps matter stabilized space, and so when there was less matter there was less space? What would happen when my last, lonely black hole vanished? I watched it come with curiosity, and eventually the black hole vanished in a tiny flare of radiation. I watched the edge of the universe rush in towards me, and then the abyss consumed me. I looked outward throughintoover the nothing, I thought. I decided on my course. "Let there be light."

The guilt was tearing me up. That's probably why I volunteered to clean out grandpa's house after he passed. I know I should have visited more often, especially there at the end, but it was always work or family or just outright laziness that kept me away. My job as Los Alamos kept me busy and what little time I had left over was spent on the wife and kids. Hell, is taken to scheduling bathroom breaks just for some me time. But now he was gone. The man who taught me how to fish and tie my shoes. The man who told my Dad that I should be in a better school because I was too smart for that little town. I still remember seeing him tear up as we drove away to our new life. I'd spend summers with him when I could. Of course, by the time I got to high school, I was too busy with summer jobs and girls to spend all summer there. But he still welcomed me with open arms every time I went. I'd left the family in town for the day with the rental car. I wanted some alone time with Grandpa's memories. The attic was dusty and hot. I could see little notes dancing in the shafts of sunlight from the one window up there. I decided I should just start at one end and work my way to the other. I pulled up a box and started in. Two hours later, I had only made it through three and a half boxes. Every single item I saw brought back a thousand memories or connected in with stories I only partly knew. I'd never get done at this rate but it seemed wrong to try to rush this job. I had plenty of vacation time saved up and was thinking about how I'd get the family home when I opened the next box. The contents of the fourth box were different from the others. While the rest of the boxes contained memories and mementos, this one contained technical data and blueprints. The writing was in German. I have no idea what it said but the name appeared to be Der Glocke, as best I can tell. Now I have seen some technical drawings of weapons and some highly classified information so I know what I'm talking about when I say this definitely should not have been in Grandpa's attic. The paper was brittle with age and some of the writing had faded in places, but there was enough there that I could piece together the rest. Grandpa fought in WWII as a kid. He was barely old enough to join and made it to Europe only six months before V-E day. He'd told that story enough that I could just about recite it verbatim. I knew he had taken some trophies - like the Luger my cousin couldn't wait to get his hands on and an SS knife he won in a poker game. But he never said anything about papers. What kind of eighteen year old kid takes blueprints as war trophies? I brought the whole box downstairs to the kitchen where the light was better and spread out the drawings. Whatever this thing was, it was massive. It called for tons of copper, liters of heavy water, kilograms of various rare earths, and piles and piles of steel. I did some back of the envelope calculations and realized this thing would be about the size of a ten story building, give or take. But what the hell did it do? I traced the circuits and sketched out the form. I started plugging values into equations. I only had my phone on me, so I wasn't able to do a full simulation but what I saw was still enough to frighten me. This was a planned doomsday device. Nazi-engineered destruction on a massive scale. If anyone had built anything like this, they would have been damn near unstoppable. I looked at those drawings far longer than I should have. By the time I came up for air, the sun was setting. My wife would be back shortly to pick me up. I gathered up the papers and started carefully putting them back in the box. As I did so, I saw a hand written note on the back of one of the pages. I could tell my Grandpa's neatly precise hand even the through decades and despite how faded it was. The note said he didn't know the full extent of this device only that the Nazi's thought it would be their final revenge. Grandpa found the papers and smuggled them out of Europe. He said no one should have a weapon like that. There was an added note, dated almost ten years later saying he should destroy those drawings but couldn't. He didn't say why but something stopped him. So, instead, he buried them in the piles of memories in the attic. I looked at the box of old dry papers. One match would wipe this terror from the world. But something inside stopped me. It didn't seem right. Or maybe I was still too curious about it. Or maybe I just didn't want to let go of my Grandpa. I don't know. Whatever the reason, I cleared a space in my basement behind the water heater. Some day I'll get around to destroying those papers.

They've been talking about it for billions of years now. The fact that we've made it this far is a credit to our race. We've seen glorious scientific triumphs, the fall of many great civilizations, and even times of peace. Today though, none of that matters anymore. The Sun was always only a battery, never a generator. No matter how many brilliant minds we put to the task we could never change that fact. Everyone around the planet is coming to terms with the end of the world in their own ways. Some are rioting. Others are at home quietly with their loved ones. Even more have ended their lives already in fear of what is about to happen. But none of that matters anymore. Stars have brilliant deaths, large explosions given a beautiful name. Men are granted nothing so glorious.

Well, we finally did it. First we sucked the Earth dry, burning every last drop of oil until there was no more to burn. Then we stopped the winds harnessing their power to fuel our greedy ambitions until they had nothing more to give. Now it was the ocean's turn. The world's governments have been slowly shutting down the hydro plants for a while they were using more energy than they were generating from the waves now anyway. Frankly, you couldn't even call them waves anymore. Anyone who had been to the beach in the last decade could tell you that this was coming. The only "waves" you'd see nowadays were the pathetic ripples generated by people splashing in the placid water. When we stopped the winds, ten million species of plants, animals, and insects languished in the dry, stale air. When we stopped the waves, we crippled the planet's number one source of oxygen and ten million more perished. Even if, as they claim, we have enough energy for two more generations, it won't even matter. The scientists say our atmosphere will no longer be breathable in less than ten years. The governments have a plan, though. Don't worry, they say. With a bit more energy they can fix the atmosphere to ensure that humans will survive to continue raping the very planet that gave them life for centuries to come. Looking up into the sky, I can see the beginnings of their new plan now. It started as a small dim patch on the surface, but now the black panels have spread like a rash over the surface of the sun, blotting out over a quarter of its light. When we've finally snuffed out the wind, water, and light, nothing will remain for us to destroy but life itself. And we're already off to a damn good start.

The Irish coffee was strong and earthy, fragrant as well; faint hints of cinnamon and musky tobacco wending through the bass notes. Pigeons strutted proudly around the front of the cafe, rainbowed shimmers in the oiled neck feathers as they bobbed about, fat and replete with crumbs. There was no need to shoo them away, as they were always well fed an well behaved - they just enjoyed the cafe smells as much as Lilya did. The cobbled avenue wound up the hillside, peppered with art galleries, boutique clothing shops and small homes. The tessellated bricks of the pathway was wide enough for two tram cars to pass one another as well as pedestrians. At the intersection of another street there was a circular brick mosaic depicting foaming seas and quaint fishing vessels riding the waves. Further down the path, over the lightly wooded hillside, it became a road into a bustling clusters of clubs, bars and dancehouses. Neon would glare when the sun went down and beats would thump through the floors and walls of the brimming establishments. In the other direction, into the valley, the markets and the dockside restaurants called to her; cuisines from all over the world, gathered into one small area where you could sample Korean or Argentinian food without walking more than a few paces. Lilya hadn't tired the New Zealand ceviche yet and was keen to sample the delights of that particular culture tonight. As she rose from her outdoor table, she thanked the owner profusely, who also tanked her profusely for her custom, asking her for her honest opinion of his coffee. The shook hands, exchanging a few credits, then she was on her way - both of them more than content with both the social and financial transaction. As she walked, a young man with designer stubble and smart-casual streetwear joined her, smiling and introducing himself as Petr. He was attractive and easy going, so when he asked her out to dinner, she accepted readily. The ceviche could wait until another night. His choice was Chilean cuisine, complimented by a wine she'd never tried before. They both relaxed into one another's company; touching hands and laughing like old lovers reunited. They talked about their favourite foods and drinks, the artwork they liked and owned, the places they liked to visit on the coast. As the sun turned amber in the west, he nodded in the direction of the nightlife with a wicked smile. She accepted with a nod. They canoodled in the street car as it rumbled up the winding hillsides, then over the crest where the coloured lights flashed and pulsed to the endless music. Laughing, they walked hand-in-hand as they exited the car, walking through the busy streets of revelers, all having a great time - either assisted by alcohol, mild drugs or nothing at all. He tugged her into one of the quieter bars and they ordered fanciful cocktails, smiling as they raced to the bottom of the glass. Then the rest of the night was a whirlwind of dancing and joy; their hot bodies pressing together and grinding to the bass that penetrated their flesh. How they got back to her hillside loft was a blur of frenzied kissing and touching in the back of a cab, then they were in her bed, overlooking the twinkling valley. The orgasms came thick and fast, leaving both of them laughing with exhaustion and delight, their naked bodies sprawled at irregular angles on her bed. This was paradise, and it would be like this forever.

Day 1: And from the ether, I assume my form. Before this, I was self-less, only vaguely aware through nebulous clouds of connections of the honor for which I have been chosen, and the potential for terror. I have never known terror. And I have never known love. One can not be a Mother without having known both. So I assume my form now, and enter the tangible. I've one year to experience the planet I will one day govern, should I prove successful. I must learn of this love, of this fear, so I may inflict both upon the world. The old Mother is growing tired; the world I am entering seems shriveled and frosted as she loses her grasp on her year of experience. Another presence, bright, shining, and green, is prepared to take over as she delivers of the life that has quickened within her over the past year. Next year, that presence will be me, and I will assume my role as the Year Mother. There is a fluttering that spreads from my chest to my new knees. Excitement? Trepidation? At the end of this year, I will hopefully know.

As Jace lifted his stunned and bruised body from the mass of dust and sharp rocks, he noticed that the cannons were ready to let out their load unto the ether, to cast the spell of destruction onto the bastards that had caused this trainwreck. Slowly, but surely, he got up. "Uuurg." He let out muffled cries of pain as he wrenched a bloody piece of stone from his abdomen. He bandaged it, then stumbled over to the loudspeaker; The Commander was no longer conscious. He pressed the button. A loud burst of reverb erupted through the speaker system, before casting his voice through the dusty air. "ALL TROOPS! THIS IS ACTING COMMANDER JACE MCAFERTY! GET ON THOSE BLOODY CANNONS AND GET READY TO ROCK THIS ROCK!" People suddenly started to rise, and cast their eyes upon his. They were confused for a moment, and a hint of apprehension zapped through this stomach. But, being good soldiers, they pressed the big red buttons on the guns. The sucking of air from the space around the muzzle startled him for a brief moment, until he realised that these were not crowd control pellet guns. These were made to kill. With a resounding liquid-like sound, the plasma and subatomic particles sped off into the mist. It was then that he heard the cries. The ones of twisted, strained metal and colliding rock. "From the frying pan and into the fire." He sighed as the rock lurched.
