"Absolutely disgusting," said Gordon, "disgusting. What the were you thinking?" "It is not for a mere mor-, I mean I thought I was making Risotto..." "This?" Gordon flings the plate into the wall. It shatters into a thousand pieces, but the Risotto stays where it was thrown, thicker than mud. "This isn't a risotto, this is a f ing disaster!" The whole kitchen holds its breath. It is not for common mortals, peasants bound to time and servitude, to talk down to the All-Father. Odin tries to stay his wrath, but the thunderstorm raging outside seems to only fuel him further. Gordon directs himself to Thor, who is on the meat counter tendering a beef with a gigantic hammer. "What is this, huh, blondie? What's this?" "I devote my time to tender this hardened meat." "With a f ing sledgehammer? Look at that thing, just, just look at it! You'll make my beef look like frozen carpet slices! Jesus, just use the meat tenderer!" "Who?" "The meat tenderer, right here!" Turning on the machine, Gordon passes the beef through it, and the magic is done - without thunders, this time. Leaving Thor to his existential crisis, he turns his attention to Loki, standing in the vegetable counter looking undecisively at..... something. "Oh, my God, what is this..... what have you done to my lettuce?" "I have arranged it." "In the shape of an owl? Why? How? How mad must you be, to waste all your f ing time making a statue out of lettuce! Lettuce! Who wants a statue made of food, tell me?" "I'd relish it." "You'd relish the sole of my boot up yours, you absolute madman! You want to waste your time so hard, go make a giant Ice statue!" "Giant? " , asks Odin, from across the room, his attention suddenly turned from trying to scrape the Risotto off the wall. "Ice? Where is it? I shall vanquish this foul beast!" And Gordon sighs, as he tries to understand how he got here. It wasn't common for him to come to New Jersey, but he always wondered why. Well, at least now he knows.

I awoke at precisely midnight on instinct alone and began fumbling around my night stand for the light switch on my lamp. Then, my brain abruptly remembered why I was roused before the nightmare my subconscious had scheduled for my R.E.M. sleep enjoyment began. I might possibly die today..... I rapidly clambered out of my bed and flicked on the room lights. As I stood there blinking furiously and adjusting to the unforgiving new glare, my thoughts gravitated towards the announcement made so many years ago..... They were ethereal, seemingly omnipotent spheres of luminescence that suddenly appeared in every sky around the world. They proceeded to boom their message into the collective consciousnesses of all of Earth's population. "Everyone will now expire on the same day as they were birthed to greater facilitate the unavoidable destiny of the universe, for better or for worse. However, your species is not deemed progressed enough to be informed of the exact year you shall perish. That is all." They disappeared in an instant and the globe erupted into chaos the next. Almost a million people died the first day, 5 times the daily average. Markets all over the world plummeted. Public services came screeching to a halt and government almost followed suite. Everyone in and out of the media had a different theory to explain what it all meant. However, it all came to a standstill on the second day when we realized what the all-powerful beings had announced was true. Everyone was dying on their birthday, with no exceptions. Even in the face of near death experiences, people would survive if it meant the laws of physics had to bend to their breaking point. As it were, war strife suddenly didn't make as much sense in this new world. Fifteen years later, violent crime is at almost zero and volatile areas across the world have steadily become more and more stable. Outside of the hit that the insurance market took initially, the global economy has reached a new all time high almost every single day. The mortality rate has remained unchanged and life expectancy is progressing as predicted so people find no reason to worry that they will die young on account of this bizarre situation. Not me..... As I finally grew accustomed to the light in my bedroom and got my bearings down, I abandoned my brief ruminations and promptly had my first anxiety attack of the day. I sprinted to my drawers and pulled out a bag. As I stood there gasping for air through a brown lunch bag, a million panicked thoughts streamed through my mind like an unstoppable river. "What if this is my year? What if someone lives longer because I die young?" On some birthdays, I even feel like running outside and going on a killing spree purely to see the writhing shock and the eventual horrifying acceptance on their faces. Who would expect to get massacred on their birthday in what is practically a post-crime society? Finally, my ragged breath evened out and I began to soothe myself to maintain composure. I banished all of the dark musings my other half brought forth and I thought of the actual likelihood that I would die today. I told myself that with a little extra precaution, I was just as safe as I was on any other day. After a stern look to myself in the mirror and a firm slap to my own face, I got ready for work and prepared to go in 5 hours early to kill time. As I left my building, I heard the oddest noise a little farther down the street towards the train station. It was a loud popping sound reminiscent of fireworks. It was strange to me because the Fourth was a few weeks ago. As I rationalized how some drunk revelers might be using up their remaining stores at 3am it hit me. The pain was immediate despite my astonishment as the bullet cleared out a cavity in my chest previously occupied by one of my lungs. As I slid to the pavement heaving blood and once again choking for air, a disheveled man ran up out of the corner of my quickly narrowing periphery. His wild eyes rolled around their sockets as he somehow grimaced and smiled at the same time. He finally looked at me long enough to triumphantly cackle, "It's MY birthday today!" I painfully turned up to him and stammered with my last breath, "M-m-m-ine too." His face went blank for a moment before he grinned and pointed his pistol straight at my head. It rested there for a second before he threw his head to the sky and began shrieking with laughter again as he bolted off. As I started slipping into the darkness of the all encompassing void, all I could think was that my breathing was slowing back down and maybe that meant everything would be alright....

Times were tough in the 20's. I was an only child and my old man had left me and my mother to chase after some vixen who promised that she'd sing to him every night after blowing him. I think back to it now, the way he described her to me, and I honestly don't blame him. My mother wasn't a looker, and she was a hell of a nagger. Me and my mom lived in the boonies outside of town in a pack of trees. Tall tuliptrees stretching so high that you had to crane your neck back to see the top of them. I had to walk about a mile through them to get to school, but I won't bore you with the whole "back in my day" business. Having no father made life growing up hard, and things got even harder. It was a rainy day in April when I came home from elementary to find my mother dead in the living room. That's a lot to put on a 13 year old, ya know? I'm no genius now, and I was even dumber then, but I knew from the marks on her throat that someone had strangled her. Well, something. I wish it was someone. There wasn't anyone to take me in; I had no family, see? Instead, after they took my poor old woman away to be roasted, I had to live in this goddamn house. Angry at the house? No, I wouldn't say that, well maybe. I loved the house before my mother died. After my mother died, see, was when I noticed it following me around. Walking to school, I could hear the branches snapping. Not on the ground, but in the trees. I'd look up into the canopy of branches of leaves, swearing on my dead mother that I heard something up there. But at first, I didn't ever see it. I'll tell you now, I'm not sure if I just didn't know what to look for, or if maybe it didn't want to be seen yet. I'm normally not the skiddish type, but after weeks of feeling something watching you from the trees, you tend to become the type who always looks over their shoulder. It became a habit of mine, looking over my right shoulder. So much so that I even did it in school even if I didn't actually hear anything. It was in high school that I finally saw it in the trees. It was for a brief second, but it was long enough to make me forget how to breathe for a few moments. It was crouched on a thick tree branch. It's skin was black and its skin was mottled. Almost looked like scales. I didn't get a good look at it's face. I probably would've died on the spot if I did. I saw it, and I know it saw me. It stood on the branch. Jesus it was so tall and lanky, you wouldn't have guessed it if you had seen it crouching first like I did. And then it leaped away through the branches like a bobcat. I ran to the sheriff and told them what I had saw, and like anyone could've guessed, he claimed that it was probably just an animal, a cat maybe. Even after describing what I had saw, he just laughed it off and said he'd send an officer over to check it out. No officer ever came. Going through the woods after seeing the damn thing made life hell. I wanted to run on my way to school, but I got the feeling that if I ran, it would chase me down, finally attacking me. So I walked. I walked and on some days I would hear it following me, leaping branch to branch. I tried to look at it several more times after building the courage, but I almost always missed it. It made me wonder if I was just imagining it, but on some days, I would catch a glimpse of it from the corner of my eye, and my stomach would turn because I knew then I wasn't just going crazy. Nowadays, it comes to the house. I can hear it crawling around on the roof at night. It knocks sometimes. I think it is trying to find a weak point. I don't know why it doesn't just come through the windows, maybe it's afraid of glass. The other night, I heard my mother's voice from the roof, despite her being a pile of ashes sitting in a jar on the mantle. Then I heard knocking on the roof again. It knew how my mother spoke. And it knocks and knocks. I don't sleep. I know if I do, it'll crash through the roof and wrap its hands around my throat, and do to me what it did to my mother. I don't sleep anymore at night. Instead I just listen to it knock. I listen to my mother calling my name.

The scene is a ship at a small island port. The wind and the angry surface of the water show signs of a storm. A middle aged man wearing a long coat is seen advancing from town and towards the ship. The shot is dark, quiet, and tense. A guard moves to stop the stranger from boarding, but the man has already drawn a gun on him and whispers "Swim boy. Swim and live." The guard hesitates, terrified, before diving off the dock and making for the coast. The scene transitions to the captain's quarters of the ship. The apparent owner of the ship is shuffling through maps, books, and notes. He hears gunfire outside and grabs his blunderbuss. He extinguishes his lamp and stands up. He is perplexed, as the gunfire, though unmistakable, sounds off. There is a strange stillness to the scene before the door is kicked in. The man in the longcoat has booted the door frame in and shot the captain in the gut. He falls backwards with a yelp, blunderbuss clattering to the floor. "Evening Richards. Care to hear a ghost story I picked up?" The man in the long coat says, kicking the fallen gun aside and striding to the lamp. Richards' eyes go wide in horror, disbelief, and agony as the lamp is turned back on. The man in the long coat's face is seen clearly for the first time. He smiles, and chuckles heartily at the fallen captain, revealing a shimmering golden upper right canine. "You're..... you're not real. I stabbed David in the gut, watched his body get pulled under by the current quick as a lightning flash. You..... you're some specter, some angel come to tell me what a great murdering bastard I've been aye?" He says between labored breaths. "Oh I'm real Richards." He said. The tip of his boot swings into his jaw, spattering blood onto the adjacent wall. "See? Still pissed off at you and all. I came here to thank you, honest. Just got all..... touchy, when I saw your ship. You know my temper though, eh Richards?" He says, kneeling so the two are at eye level when he playfully slaps at the captain's cheek. Richards gasps and wheezes before succumbing to shock and blacking out. David jams a needle into Richards' thigh that brings him gasping to life. "Richards..... I thought you killed me too. But that current took me some place you wouldn't believe. I'm gon na show you, so you know what you unleashed on this earth before I put three more bullets in you." "I still don't believe it. You're not. You can't. You..... he died..." David stands up, gun in one hand aimed at Richard's chest, other hand held up, middle finger and thumb pressed together. The room begins to shake, and the storm outside suddenly unloads on the port and town. The room fills with an eerie purple light, wind tearing through the small room with all the force of a hurricane. A hum in the background grows almost overwhelming, nearly drowning out the storm in the cabin and outside. The scene transitions with the sound of a finger snap. It's day. The ship is now docked outside of a small, modern day tourist trap beach. David grabs Richards and thrusts his head through the remains of the window overlooking the town. "You should thank me Richards. This is where we grew up, you and I, two hundred years after the day your ship disappeared from existence. I've blessed you little brother. Who else on this earth has this privilege?" Richards is speechless, gawking at the sheer unfamiliarity of the landscape before him. He's thrown back on the floor and the gun is jammed against his forehead. "You and I both know this is a long time coming. Last words? Might interrupt you, but humor me." Richards moved to say something when a finger snap is heard. A second David appears, wearing a business suit. He kicks the gun from the first David's hand, grabs Richards, and disappears with another snap of his fingers. David is now alone and dumbfounded. He sighs, hard and frustrated, trying desperately to keep his anger down. He calmly picks up his gun, massaging his wrist, and sits down in the captain's chair, massaging the bridge of his nose. He throws the table over and fires the gun's last five bullets into the ceiling, screaming a percussive "Fuck" with each shot. He gathers himself, laughing, reloading, and lighting a cigar. The screen cuts to black with a last snap. The credits begin to roll.

He came to his senses suddenly, flinching from where he had lain seconds before. He felt his eyes adjusting to the painfully bright light, which coated the entire room in a sterile white. The man looked down upon himself and realized that he was, in perspective to the ordeal he had experienced last, relatively unscathed. An involuntary sigh of relief and both apprehension escaped his chest. A barrage of questions from his mind fired upon him at once. "Where am I?" "Where are the others?" "Did we succeed?" His muscles tightened and he stood up, walking over to the edge of the room. There were no doors and no windows. He led his fingers along the white, blank surface of the wall and felt for something, a switch, a button, a bump, anything. As if on cue, the wall before his hands parted in two and revealed yet another corridor. Just as he had taken two swift steps, he heard a click. Swirling around and instinctively reaching for his belt, he realized bitterly that all his former possessions were gone. Before him stood a man or a humanoid, for lack of a better word. It was as if the divine being which shaped man after himself took his own features and altered them each just enough for them to be noticeable. The humanoid held a long, oblong object which the man assumed to be a weapon. "Dammit. Alright, you got me, I surrender," he says as he cautiously raises his hands, showing that he is unarmed. The humanoid remains still and silent, staring at him with an uneasy yet curious gaze. "Do you understand what I'm saying? Fuck, do you guys even talk? Can you at least say something?" Absolute silence. "Look, I've got no weapons. I'm no threat," he gestured slowly towards the object grasped by the humanoid. He then pointed towards himself, showing that he, unlike the thing that stood across from him in the hallway, was clearly unarmed. The humanoid seemed to gain some amount of comprehension and lowered his weapon. He gestured with a sudden twitch of his head, still not uttering a single sound. Noticing that the alien began to walk slowly towards the end of the hallway, the man delicately took a few steps after it. The alien looked at him with further interest, so he assumed that the humanoid wanted him to follow. They stepped into another room, which appeared to have something that resembled two stools and a table. A blank screen appeared on the table. The humanoid approached the screen and began furiously tracing his fingers or what appeared to fill the function of fingers across the screen, forming patterns of shapes and symbols. "Touch-screen, huh? Guess you guys aren't as backwards as we made y'all out to be." He tried to get a closer look at what it was drawing, but the thing wouldn't allow him to see it. He patiently waited, and after what seemed like an hour, the thing abruptly stopped and looked at him. The man approached the screen. There was a big circle. Their planet. Crude stick figure-like markings. Probably them too. The next few drawings showed what the man could only imagine to be their culture, how they lived, how they gathered food, celebrated, mourned, fought, and loved. The final drawings were done much hastier. It showed what appeared to be star ships in the sky, raining drops of fiery destruction and chaos upon the land. The stick figures were no longer so animated in their depictions. They were dead. Tears formed in his eyes like condensation formed among the clouds, fell on his face like the rain droplets fell through the sky, like the droplets of uranium and napalm in the drawings, splattered on his hands like the soft kiss of the rain on a child's face, like the lifetimes of awareness and consciousness terminated by humanity's arrogance. A wave of remorse, guilt, and comprehension hit the man. "You don't understand..... our planet is dying. We had to find a way to survive. I just followed orders." He closed his eyes and new tears flowed down the crevices of the wrinkles on his face, knowing all too well that it the thing the sentient, breathing, compassionate being before him would not understand. They would never understand it was simply too late. A bang and its vibrations reverberated through the walls of the spaceship. His salvation had come, albeit at the expense of the life before him.

"Warning, centrifugal force, decreasing..... engine failing" "Major Addams, we need to fix this ASAP..... if we don't, we'll lose control of the ship and we'll be left floating in space..." Commanded General Stephenson. "With all due respect, Sir, we're running out of options. We've only got half of our team left..... and we're getting our asses chewed in this asteroid storm; we need everyone manning the flight consoles!" Shouted Addams. The ship takes a violent hit, sending the two men careering to the floor. "Yeah, some job they're doing! Send Farmer down to the engine room, he's our best shot." Demanded Stephenson. "But sir, we'll never..." Stephenson cut in, "That's an order, Addams..... get to it!" Addams high tails it down the corridor of the Traverse IV, the fourth ship to leave Earths solar system and explore beyond. The alarms are screeching, layering more pressure upon Major Addams psyche. "Sargent Farmer! You've got to get down to the engine room and stabilise the centrifugal unit, Generals orders!" Cried Addams. "Sir, we're almost out of the asteroid field!" Replied Farmer, sounding relieved. "Nice work, I'll take over..... Farah, Rodriguez; eyes up, let's get past this last wave!" The crew do their best to avoid the asteroids, taking more heavy hits; the armour is beyond repair and cosmic radiation is flooding the ship. "Almost..... there, how are they doing on the starboard side!?" Addams shouts. "Sir! That part of the ship is redundant now, the safety protocol sealed the doors and locked us out, with no way to override it! Kennedy is down, the radiation fried him..... fuck, this is bad, there are still others in there!" Screamed Rodriguez. "Damn it! All right, focus on getting out of here..." The alarms are still screeching and the crew are still pounding the flight consoles in order to evade destruction. "Shit, Addams, we've got a big one..... we're done for!" Farah cries. "Underneath it, go underneath it! Come on, all systems go!" The asteroid is heading directly towards the Traverse, this collision will be fatal. "We're out of time! Brace for impact!!" Farah screams. The ship is pounded, glass and metal rain down on the crew; the back up shutters kick in and close any compromised areas; shielding them from the vacuum. All thrust is lost and the ship is left adrift, lifeless; as if it were another piece of space debris. "A..... Addams? Can you hear me? We're the only ones left on this deck; we need to get to the bridge, it's the only place that hasn't been compromised!" Shouts Farah desperately. She makes to pick Addams up, but he's useless; his limbs are like jelly. After a few moments, he comes back round. "Farah..... Farah, we need to go, I can taste the metallic essence of the radiation, Jesus..... we'll fry here! Fuck, Rodriguez!" He gets up from the floor, dazed and disorientated. They head towards the central corridor which leads to the bridge. They stumble towards the heavy doors and operate the console. They make their way in to find General Stephenson and some other crew members. "Did you hear from Farmer?" Spluttered Addams. "He's gone, Major..... he was crushed in the engine room." The General replied, with an annoying calmness in his voice. "Fuck! If only..." Addams was interrupted again. "He died following orders, he died serving the very honour of our ship." Spits the General. Addams and Farah sit on a nearby crate; looking out of the large window. The haze of space dust doesn't offer much of a view for now. "Where are we?" Asks another crew member. "Well, soldier, we've actually broken the galactic border; the ships heat sensors are through the roof, according to this; we've reached a humongous mass of space dust. I can't explain it. But, we've taken such a beating we can't move to observe." The General replies. "Um..... Major Addams..... what the hell, is that?" Farah is glued to the window; the dust clears and behind it lies a gigantic, oval shaped rock; so huge it makes Jupiter look like a pinhead. "What..... General?" There is an eerie silence in the room. "I'll be damned..... the fourth ship sent out for space exploration, and we finally make it past the edge of our galaxy. This is what lays beyond..." The oval shaped rock is surrounded by an array of moons, asteroids, stunning super novas and space storms. "What in the world..... what do we do?" Farah asks. "We wait." The General replies. "The mass of this Titan, pl..... whatever it is, is slowly pulling us in; we'll find out in time. For now, we're the universe's." "I'll try to make contact back to Earth! I'll try and bounce the frequencies off of the radiation to relay a message!" Shouts Addams. The Traverse IV is left, drifting towards this gigantic rock; awaiting their fate, they have no idea what this place holds.

"Hey Mom...... did you hear about the news? Mars is actually the original planet that humans evolved on!" "How fascinating!" Emily took her son's phone and held it several feet from her face, squinting uncomfortably through the bottom of her glasses. "Take off your shoes, honey. Remember when I told you about our global crisis? How the United World Leaders Alliance banned plastic and fossil fuels and how the atmosphere stabilized." "How old were you?" Brennan asked, fascinated. "I was three when the UWLA was founded," Emily replied, scrolling as she read the article. "There was a lot of people who thought that global warming was unfounded, but "HA!" Grandpa staggered into the room, holding his own tablet. "You see the news? We used to live on Mars?" "Yes, Father," said Emily, looking resigned. "I know you don't believe that climate change was an issue "This proves it wasn't!" Grandpa shouted with all the self-important flamboyance of vindication. "See? Those Cassandran dumbasses were wrong-there WAS a Planet B!"

" Seems like the right weather for this, doesn't it, " Neil Raymond asked his son. The sky was grey and dried leaves skittered lazily across the lawn. Neil bent down and picked two red-tinged leaves out from the narrow hole that he had dug a foot deep. They crunched softly in his hand as he discarded them to the side, and wiped his hand on the side of his pants. Brian, a dark-haired 7-year-old stood next to him wearing a pair of kakis, a blue button up shirt and a red clip-on tie. In his hands he held a small, skinny shoe box, on the side the word ' Converse'had been crossed out with magic marker and over the star on top a piece of masking tape read ' Monster.'He looked up at his father and asked, " Do I just start talking? " " Whenever you're ready, buddy, " Neil responded, placing a hand on his son's shoulder. Brian looked down at the box and then at Neil, " Can you hold it? I need to read my apology. " Neil smiled, " Eulogy, bud, you're reading a eulogy. " He took the box and held it against his side as he waited for his son to produce his piece of paper. Brian dug through his pants pockets, the familiar sound of Lego clattering together competing with the rustling leaves. Finally he is holding a hastily-folded piece of paper with the scratchy handwriting Neil was so used to checking over for errors. Brian fiddled with his tie, making it more crooked than before; he cleared his throat and began to read " Today we are here to bury the monster from my room. Mom and dad said it was just my imagination, but it was just real good at hiding. It was too smart to get caught in the mouse traps and it only came out when it was real dark. It would wake me up scratching on the walls and moving stuff under my bed but would stop when I turned the lights on. " A few drops of rain dotted his paper and the wind started to come in stronger gusts. " Sorry, Brian, we might want to wrap this up pretty quick here, " Neil suggested. " Ok, dad, " Brian said with a little disappointment. He cleared his throat again, " I guess from now on I don't have to be afraid of monsters in my room, because I know how to get ' em. They don't expect it when it's still dark. So long, monster; sorry I had to kill you. " He folded his paper back up and walked over to Neil, taking the box back. The box fell into the hole with a thud and Brian pushed the now wet dirt on top, stomping on the mound and leaving size three-and-a-half prints. His father laughed slightly, " Leave it to you to get filthy no matter what. Let's go in and get cleaned up, mom will be home soon. You did a wonderful job. " - Neil stood at the sink washing his hands and looking out at the small patch of flattened dirt outside the window. As he was drying them off he heard the front door close and his wife walking into the kitchen. " Give me a hand putting these away, will you? " Wendy asked, setting down two heavy canvass bags of groceries. " How did everything go? " After thinking for a moment Neil said " You know it went really well. I thought that what he wrote was pretty nice but he had to skip a bit when it started raining. He still has it written down, I'll have him read it to you after his bath. " " After his bath? Didn't he take one before getting all dressed up, " Wendy asked surprised. Neil laughed, " You know your son, if there's dirt to be had he'll make sure he has it. I've got his pants soaking downstairs. " " It looks like he's not the only one, " Wendy said, pointing to the side of his paints. " What is that, tree sap? " Neil looked down to see a dark green stain on the side of his pants, smeared just below his pocket, looking like it had dripped down when it was wet. Touching it with his hand it was slightly tacky and stayed on his fingers. " I don't know, " he said, bringing his fingers up to his nose. After a sniff he cringed, almost retching. " Whatever it is it smells like rotten meat. " " You probably did it when you took out the trash when I left. You better go put them in with Brian's pants. I'll get started on dinner. " Wendy put away the last of the groceries and put a pot of water on the stove. - Neil scrubbed away at the dark stain while more water ran into the laundry sink. ' I didn't notice any hole in the bag when I got rid of the trash,'he thought to himself. Shrugging he tossed pushed the pants under the soapy water, dried his hands and went back upstairs. As he walked past the back door he noticed it was slightly open into the hallway, one of Brian's habits. On the outer knob he saw his son's handprint in that same dark green that he had just been scrubbing. " Well, that solves that mystery, " said Neil, chalking it up any of the multitude of sticky things a seven-year-old manages to find on a daily basis. As he pushed the door closed he saw a piece of garbage tumble across the back patio. Thinking that he forgot to put the lid on the trash can, one of his own habits, he went out after it. It was a piece of cardboard, now blown against the fence. He picked it up and started towards the trash can but stopped when he looked at it. One side was filthy, but the off-white strip stuck to the center seemed to repel the dirt. The lettering was unmistakable, across the tape in thick black marker read the word ' Monster.'

" Don't do it. " For years I had been receiving visions. Visions of a brighter future. A future where the worries of today; famine, war, poverty, were nightmares relegated to obscurity. A world where every man, woman and child could live out their lives in peace and harmony, free from the uncertainty that plagued them, free from fear. A world where I could be happy. " Stop before it's too late. " It started when I was five, the day my mother died, as I shuddered in fitful sleep. I'd woken in the to the sound of deep, heavy breathing. I'd opened by eyes and found myself face-to-face with a man, his hair streaked with white, his eyes lit with a deep knowing energy. Needless to say I screamed, I struggled, I tried to run. I couldn't move. I blinked. He was gone. The days went by, the months, and with each day came a night, and with each night came the nightmares, and with each nightmare I awoke to the same face, silent the save the sound of his breath. I started to believe I was broken, damaged. I told my dad and he laughed, returning to the bottle. I told my friends, pleaded with them to believe me, they thought me strange and abandoned me. I don't blame them. I told my teachers, they sent me to a shrink, who diagnosed me with mild parasomnia brought on by anxiety. He was wrong. Two years passed and the man started talking, telling me strange and wondrous tales. I lay there and listened, time immaterial in the darkness, to the path he put before me. At first I felt nothing but fear, but his stories pulled me in, designed as they were to entice and bewilder, simple in their execution but with a gravitas that I was unable to appreciate when I was so young. The tales he told, of great Kings, Conquerors that controlled the world, Knights that roamed far and wide performing deeds of good, finally helped me sleep. Five years passed and I was no longer afraid. The man had been there for me, through the years, helping me through the night. His stories had been replaced by direct guidance, wise words whispered that gave me what my father could not. He taught me how to manipulate, what to say in every situation, how to succeed. I went from a waif, drifting through childhood from detention to detention, to the popular kid in school, beloved by all. I could do anything. Fifteen years passed and the guidance now came with visions. The meaning was clear. " Do this and you will be great. " " Do this and you will succeed. " " Do this and you will get your heart's desire. " His true nature was clear to me now, he was me. A wiser me. An older me. I became successful, starting my own company. I became driven, growing and expanding. I was a bright young star that could not be ignored, and being a star comes with opportunity. I grew wealthy, I grew powerful. Thirty years passed and it wasn't enough. I had ascended the corporate ladder, it wasn't enough. I had run for office, it wasn't enough. I'd started charities, helped people, and for awhile the work had sated me, but it wasn't enough. The man in the dreams still came, but now he looked back at me in every mirror, the white streaks of hair that seemed so strange now a permanent reminder of who I'd become. I still listened, and still he guided, but the guidance had changed. " What are you missing? " " When were you last truly happy? " " There's one thing you still need. " I had to get it. Thirty-one years have passed and now I stand here on the precipice, the ice cold rain running down my body as I stare at the mound before me bathed in moonlight. He is here, different, true, but still a version of me, his clothes dishevelled, his face gaunt. " Please, this will be the end of us, stop. " I brush my hand over the stone, sweeping aside the vines and dust. The lettering worn but legible. " Here rests Grace, loving mother to her son, wife to her husband, taken cruelly before her time. " I raise my shovel.

Why does this always happen to me? I felt water trailing my forehead and continuing down beneath the hairline. Cold. Something drummed beside my head. Where was I? A gray, foggy landscape appeared before my eyes. One blink, two blinks. A world emerged through the fog, the gray landscape changing into a pouring, cloudy sky. Still blinking away the raindrops, I tried to sit up. My hands fumbled over cold brick, slippery and rough. Dirt and stones seemed to find their way into all of the small cuts and cracks. In the vertical world all of my senses suddenly seemed to return. A police siren wailed in the distance, partly distorted by rain and traffic. Neon signs proclaimed messages of beer, wine and spirits. A couple of yards away a small crowd had begun to assemble. They pointed in my direction. Both angry voices and giggles found their way through the city noise. I was used to it. My naked body had a tendency to attract the eyes of curious peers, especially when I as now, sat alone in the street with a puzzled look all over my face. A flickering light in the corner of my eye stole my attention. A tattered newspaper shone in front of a cold fluorescent light, partly wet behind its broken glass. " Italy declares war" . Today's date - 10 June, 1940. A longer trip than last time in other words. What was I doing here? Why do I keep doing this to myself, over and over? Slowly I searched my body for the tattoo. First the legs, then my stomach, chest and arms. Different places every time. Bleak outlines surrounded the pale skin that had previously contained similar messages. This time the ink could be found on the back of my right forearm. "22:17, 40.782948, -73.973756." Without spilling any time I stood up and headed towards the ever-increasing crowd of people. First time posting here! I originally wrote it in Swedish, why not improve your writing in two languages as well as your translation skill?;) For the interested reader I will paste the original as well: Varfor hander det har alltid mig? Jag kande hur en stril av vatten rann langs pannan och ner inunder harfastet. Kallt. Nagonting smattrade hogljutt I narheten av mitt huvud. Var var jag? Ett dimmigt gratt landskap uppenbarade sig framfor ogonen. En blinkning, tva blinkningar. Varlden tradde fram ur dimman, det graa landskapet var en molntackt himmel som oppnat sig. Blinkandes av regndropparna forsokte jag satta mig upp. Mina hander trevade langs med kalla gatstenar, hala och skrovliga. Grus tycktes leta sig in I alla sprickor och sar. I den vertikala varlden tycktes genast alla sinnen hitta tillbaka. En polissiren hordes I fjarran, delvis drankt I regn och biltrafik. Neonskyltar proklamerade budskap om ol, vin och sprit. En bit bort borjade en mindre folkmassa ansamlas. De pekade I min riktning. Bade arga roster och fnitter hittade sin vag genom stadens sorl. Jag var van. Min nakna kropp hade en tendens att dra till sig blickar, speciellt nar jag som nu satt ensam pa en gata som ett levande fragetecken. Ett flimmer till vanster om mig stal min uppmarksamhet. En trasig tidningsannons lystes upp av ett kallt lysrorssken bakom krossat glas. " Italien forklarar krig! " . Dagens datum - 10 juni, 1940. Langre resa an sist med andra ord. Vad gjorde jag har? Varfor utsatter jag mig sjalv for det har, gang pa gang? Langsamt finkammande jag min kropp efter tatueringen. Forst benen, sedan magen, brostet och armarna. Olika stallen varje gang. Svaga konturer omgav blek hud som tidigare hade innehallit liknande meddelanden. Den har gangen fanns blacket pa baksidan av min hogra underarm. " 22:17, 40.782948, -73.973756 ." Utan att spilla nagon tid stallde jag mig upp och tog riktning mot den standigt okande skaran av manniskor.

They talk over me. Mouths, dripping and spraying the remnants of the dinner I had spent hours on, uttering nonsense neither one was listening to. Overlapping threads of internal conversations competing against one another in an endless battle that had no winner. " Can I go to Jerome's on Friday? " Queries the smaller one sitting to my right. " You spent all day playing on your iPad. None of your chores are done! What did you do all day? " The larger one avoids answering directly. I stare out the window as a neighbor slowly walks along the sidewalk edging our yard, my mind sneaking alongside him engaged in a polite conversation around whether it was a morning dove or pigeon we heard cooing in the distance. " I want a FIFA 15 for my birthday. " The threads of the conversation jumped at random angles to one another. I listen, gauging when they're close enough for me to bind together for a moment. " Well, your birthday isn't for another month. How about you start a list and keep adding - " My voice is drowned out by the larger mouth. " Another video game!? That's ridiculous! " I've managed to bind the threads of conversation again, but the energy is too difficult to contain. " I wanted to go the SportsClub, but you wouldn't take me yesterday!? " Replies the smaller mouth. " Don't change the subject! Did you apologize to your mother for talking back last night? " The Larger is unaware of the tangential nature of his own comments. The conversation has played itself over again and again. Invisible would be a step up. I'm more a wall, something to be talked over or avoided. But never actively engaged with. The neighbor glances at our window and I smile. He knows. He knows me. I stand up, before the momentary impetus leaves me. If it's one thing I've learned from the two next to me, is that consideration is for those who want to slow themselves. And I do not. " Goodbye Karl. " I give the larger mouth a peck on the cheek. I give the small mouth a squeeze of the shoulder. The damage of leaving is less than staying. I don't grab a bag. I don't grab the keys. I simply stride forward with a purpose I haven't felt in decades and put my hand on the doorknob, twisting hard. I've used this door a thousand times, but for the first time I use it as the exit.

He stepped out of the portal and entered the shop through the front door. Making his way between the stacks, he found the section he was looking for, "Historical," and grabbed the newest looking edition he could see. He opened it to a random page, and noticed a discrepancy; that wasn't how it went at all. After all, he'd been at that war- watched it unfold before him! He surmised it had to be an editing mistake. Flipping to another random section, toward the end of the book, he noticed more mistakes, these ones showing extreme biases toward another people- against the ones who had lost that particular war during their era. He shook his head. Wandering over to another section, he figured maybe if the references were mistaken, then surely "Educational" would be accurate. How can they teach something untrue, after all? Picking up the brief introductory edition, he opened to yet another random page, and saw that not only were they teaching the mistakes, they were citing the biases as fact. He paused again, and sighed. Typical. It really is the same way it has always been, and always will be. The winners write the history books, and anything contrary is a lie. Just like now.

And yet, the city remained. Our final landmark. Nobody remembers the first day. Why? Because it was just a normal day. The gentle, seemingly harmless coughing was disguised among the rest of the world. And everybody was unknowing. A stranger unknowingly infecting a passerby. A husband unknowingly dooming his wife. A mother unknowingly killing her newborn. There's no hope for a cure when it goes unnoticed. We can not stop what we can not predict. It spread everywhere. Introverts, extroverts, children, teens, adults, even animals. After ten minutes patient zero was among thousands. The fourth day. The final woman, 22, surrounded by nobody - void of motivation. Possibly immune but it didn't matter now. Within seconds she hit the ground. No pain. On the fifth day, the city had no economy. It had no traffic. It had no concerts or comedy shows. It had no laughing or crying or screaming. No happiness. No love. No sadness. Humanity was gone. And yet, the city remained.

" What are you going to do, kill me? " A tired young man cresting the hill paused for a moment, smiling at my words. " I've been following you for four-and-a half months; I had time to contemplate the problem, " began the young man, leaning on a spear that appeared in good condition despite its apparent recent service as a walking stick. " If Death (Blessed be His Name) rejects you from his presence, I can hardly force you to share your Reasons. " I smiled. They usually had time to think. It was one of the reasons I kept moving, otherwise the real idiots caught up and, well..... tried to kill an invulnerable man so he would teach them the secret to immortality. Little shits. Still, this one was, at least, vaguely amusing. " It's a problem really. If I tell you, if I tell anyone, " I explained, " they might share the secret, then everyone might start using it. Of course, I don't know if that would even matter; if He'd thank me for saving Him time in his appointed tasks, or if He'd be pissed I ruined his little game. And even then, don't know if Death gets bored, but really, why should I take the risk for you people? " The young man looked taken aback. " I didn't know what to you'd be like, " he said conversationally. " I didn't really expect you to be an arrogant bastard though. Isn't immortality supposed to give you serenity and enlightenment or something? " " Bah, " I responded. " Maybe with some gods it does. Death's a stingy prick, apparently. " Blinking, the young man - a soldier perhaps? - loped forward. " I..... didn't expect you to be so..... " he fumbled for words. " Dickish? " I offered. He seemed to agree. " Yeah, it turns out there's no need for manners when I literally can't die. " " I considered torture, you know, " he ventured. " The smarter ones get around to it eventually, " I agreed. " It's been tried before. I've been whipped, beaten, hanged, stabbed, even killed once I think. I'm a little fuzzy about a few days in there. Some idiots got creative with some spikes and a tree. " The young man shuffled closer, his eyes catching - only for a moment, to his credit - on my scars. I don't blame him - my body was littered with wounds. From my hands to my toes. " A few times I even broke. I told them my Reason. " I shrugged. " It hasn't ever seemed to help anyone. " " So..... " he paused, a rueful grin blooming across his face, " you going to tell Me? " I turned and began walking away, reveling as disappointment eroded his good cheer. " I used to make up the same desperate reasons you all do every morning. But one day I woke up and decided That Bastard isn't worth it. And that day I decided if he wants me today, then screw it. And every day since then I've woken and told that Divine Dick one thing:..... " The young man seemed to pause, hopeful, even as I walked away. And, realizing that he was a screwball anyway, I turned and told him, " I Am. "

You step forward, concentrating your powers on the girl before you. She remains silent, fearful of both your appearance and of those around her. It's her first day here. "I'd like a number one with no onions," you say. You can feel her stutter coming on. To avoid making her feel even more skittish, you pre-empt her by adding, "A small, for here. That will be it." "Seven ninety-five," she says at last. You hand her your bank card - or maybe it's just a really good fake of one, you haven't quite figured it out yet but no one's called you out on it thus far so it seems like a moot point - and payment for your purchase is processed quickly. She hands you a receipt. "Your order number is 83 and will be ready shortly," you both say simultaneously, her voice trailing off in the last few words, unnerved by your uncanny prediction of her exact phrasing. You attempt to take the empty cup she offers you, but while your hands are normally guided by the eyes of those around you, you have only the girl's mind to rely upon and she doesn't seem to have sufficient spatial awareness, leading you to fumble around on the counter, groping for your cup. One messy soda machine escapade later, you're sipping on a delicious lemon-lime beverage, your hand dripping in several other flavors. Your order comes ready, and you take it to an unoccupied table and begin to eat. Your phone rings. You answer it, covering it in sugary stickiness despite your best attempts to dry your hands earlier. "DETECTIVE, WE NEED YOU," bellows the man on the other end of the line. Lieutenant Kite of the 25th Precinct. You didn't need your powers of omniscience for that one, but you quickly ponder using them later to obtain his Social Security number. "THERE'S THIS CRIMINAL THEY CALL'THE INVISIBLE MAN' AND "I'm at lunch, Lieutenant," you snap, perturbed. "I've still got another 32 minutes. Union rules. Don't interrupt me again." You angrily hammer the end call button. You unwrap your burger and take a bite. Onions.

THE CLERK: Case on trial, all rise for the Honorable Newland. THE COURT: Thank you, the people will continue with their examination of Detective Townsend at this time. (Whereupon Detective Bruce Townsend took the stand and was resworn) Q. Thank you your honor. Now, Detective Townsend, are you familiar with the term "consciousness transfer." A. Yes. Q. Could you explain what a consciousness transfer is to the jury? A. Well, a consciousness transfer is a relatively recently approved form of capital punishment. I don't know all the medical details of how it works, but, the process essentially involves transferring the prisoner's consciousness into that of their victim. They essentially live out their victim's last 24 hours, and when the victim dies, so does the prisoner. The prisoner has no control over what happens. They just see and hear what the victim saw, heard, and thought. Q. Is there anything else that happens during a consciousness transfer? A. Yes, well, we - - I mean it is possible for the police to view the consciousness transfer. We can see what the prisoner sees, what the victim saw, on a monitor. Q. Why are consciousness transfers only used as capital punishment? A. The transfer is irreversible. Once it is started, it can not be stopped. You are in their consciousness until they die, and at that point you die as well. Also, the person who the person whose consciousness the prisoner is being transfer too must be dead. We can't send anyone the the consciousness of a living person. Q. Okay. Have you, in your capacity as a detective ever viewed a consciousness transfer? A. Yes. Q. Approximately how many? A. I would say over 100. Q. Did you view the consciousness transfer of Stephanie Sam, on January 18, 2057? A. Yes. Q. What had Ms. Sam been sentenced to death by consciousness transfer for doing. What happened? A. Well, Ms. Sam had been convicted of the murder of 85 year old mother. The victim had been killed by blunt force trauma to the head. The victim had recently informed Ms. Sam of her intention to cut Ms. Sam out of her substantial will. Q. And what did you see while viewing the consciousness transfer? A. I saw the victim's death through her own eyes. I saw her murderer. Q. And do you see this person in the room today? A. Yes, he is sitting in the blue suit over there. Q. Let the record reflect the witness has identified the defendant, Alan Greco, your honor.

"Hello, Timmy." Santa said softly, his beard rustling. But his voice cut through the silence like a sharp knife. "Satan." I stated. "Not him, no. I'm Santa. Santander Clausula, but you kids know me as Santa Claus." "What? I summoned Satan! I wrote his name!" "Timmy boy, you are severely dyslexic. I'm surprised the scripture even understood what you wrote. But I'm so glad you have tried to write. So proud. But why have you tried to summon the darkness into your beloved home?" "It's.... It's my dyslexia. I don't want it. I want to be normal! Like the other kids!" "No, Timmy. You are better than normal. You have to accept who you are, and embrace yourself. You've had a some bad times, but I didn't put you on my naughty list. Because I see your heart, and it's purer than a baby's butt." I giggled. Baby butts are stinky, not pure. But that wasn't the point. "But the other kids are laughing at me! I want to make myself better, so I can play with them." A pause. "Timmy, do you know Bill?" "Yeah. He's the one that makes fun of me because I can't read right." I said sadly. "Want to know a secret?" "What?" "His parents are going through some difficult times." "Divorce?" "At worst. How would you feel if your parents are fighting all the time?" I thought for a bit. "Worried?" I tried. "Yes. Worried and angry. There's nothing he can do about it except be constantly frustrated by his helplessness." Santa waited a moment for it to sink in. "But why is he bullying me?" "Remember that time your sister took your lego piece and wouldn't give it to you back. And you were angry all day. And you punched the pillow in your tree house a few times?" Santa asked. "Yes, but what does that have to do with anything?" "You took your anger out on the pillow. Bill took his anger on you." "But that's not fair! It's not my fault what's happening to his family!" "People cope with their problems and anger differently. What Bill did wasn't right. But you have to understand his situation. He wants things to be normal, like you do." I was starting to think I knew where Santa was coming from. "Just be patient, Timmy. And listen to your parents. Don't dwell in these ancient scriptures. Dyslexia isn't the end of the world." He said, rising from the summoning circle. "In fact," he continued, "Rudolph is dyslexic, too." and with that, he left through the chimney.

"I need a game that a kid would like!" he shouted frantically as he entered the store, "A little girl." "X-box or play station?" barked the clerk from across the store. "Neither" he shouted back "We have a sale on consoles right now. That would be a great gift" "I'm not buying her a damn console. Something cheap she'll like," he said, getting frustrated, "And quickly, please." "Here, Sims. Just came out," The clerk said, game in hand, "It'll run on any computer from this decade." "Great! I'll take it. Can you wrap it?" he said, checking his watch. "Fuck." "FUCK!" James bashed his steering wheel. This was not the first time that he had fucked up; but forgetting his own daughter's birthday. That was truly a new low. He left work early, trying to surpise her by coming home before her, hopefully a nice gesture. As he pulled up to his small house and ran inside. He checked his watch, 3:20. "They should be back," he said as he marched through the door. But nothing. The house was empty, and in the kitchen he saw a note propped up against a dozen empty bottles. He opened it and it read "I'm leaving and I'm taking Lizzy. Don't try to find us." His heart dropped. "No!" he shouted. He ran up the stairs to find his room a mess and his closet empty. In his daughters room, nothing. Even the bed sheets were gone. "Her mother," he whispered, they have to be there. He dialed her number, then again, and again. No answer. "Fuck!" he yelled for no one to hear. "Did she give her the idea. That bitch never liked me. Fuck!" He almost drove to her house before remembering the note. The shock faded and terror set in. It was over, everything was over. He willed himself to move, step by step, to the garage, pulling one bottle of scotch and drinking as much as he could before heading to the tv. Every part of his body shivered with anxiety as he took another sip from the bottle. His nightly routine started a bit early tonight. He woke up with a gun in his hand. He thought to himself exactly what he had planned to do with it. Awful was the thought that he was going to kill himself, but he was physically repulsed when he thought what he might've done to his wife. The wife he knew he loved, but hated. That was it. He poured the entire case down the drain, along with anything he had in the fridge. He was cutting out the single thing that ruined his life. That ruined him. The first night was easy, the second harder. He took the week off work hoping less stress would make it easier, but it gave him little to do. "Life is boring when you stop drinking," he thought to himself with a smirk on his face. He threw the game into the computer. " 'Anything from this decade,' thats what he said." Then the game booted up. He had played once before, his daughter showed him the family she had built. He remembered feeling weird when she used the word. "You dont built a family." Then, with no warning, the game started. Voices faintly spoke from the machine as images of people walked around a 3 story house. "If only it was that easy." He explored the game, doing the things his daughter had showed him. Making the family cook, clean, work. Motonous daily activities. He hated it. James left for the TV. Less thought. He figured that getting through the day was all that was important, and without thinking he could get through the day. But after an eternity of stupid shows, sports, and news he checked the clock. 10:30. "Fuck," he whispered to himself. James had began to realize how often he had said that. So he went back to the computer. The game was still running, and he saw the computer person doing something perculiur; it was taking a smoke break. A game for kids, and it was smoking. But James had another idea, he could use this character to do all the things that he had never done. First was smoking. He was still baffled that this "thing" would smoke in a kids game. Next was..... nothing. He watched this thing sitting at a desk for almost ten minutes before he could even think of something to make it do. "A casino," he thought. He had never gambeled with anything other than scratch-offs. He had the thing leave the building and drive to the casino. Hours of loosing before James had realized that there was no point to a virtual casino. There is nothing to win. Nothing real he can loose. So he decided to leave. Both the game and James' world were dark. As the thing walked out, he was propositioned. "Ten buck for a joint," the shady looking man said audibly through the game. Dumbfounded, James decided to take it. Smoking pot was another thing he had never done. The game became odd. Oddly accurate. The man's driving was significantly worse, and speaking to his wife was slower and more incoherent than anything said before. "A fucking kids game" he shouted. Then anxiety washed over him when he remembered why he had bought the game in the first place. He wanted a drink. But that was what got him here in the first place. Then he got back to the game. Realizing that he could controll the entire family, Husband, wife, and son, he switched to the wife. She was cooking dinner when the husband came home. She had stopped to yell at the husband for smoking, and the pot on the stove began to boil over. "Go and fix it," he commanded. But then another thought. Why did he make her do that. There are no repercussion, nothing of value can be lost. The game was like the casino. So he decided to go a different route with his playing. Not things he would want to do, but rather things he would never do. But not tonight. James went to bed, having a tough time with the slowly growing headache. In the morning he opted to skip breakfast for another 10 minutes at the computer. He started the game up to see that the people were still sleeping, when an odd command appeared under his cursor. James couldn't resist clicking it, and just as commanded the wife disappeared under the covers, and the husband quickly awoke. "Lucky him," James murmured to himself. That morning he followed the girl, and with his new plan and improved skill, decided to make her more..... outgoing. He watched her go to work, which he found incredibly boring. An accounting firm. Again, he was stunned how this game was given to him for a kid. Then he decided to take control. "A strip club!" he thought. She left work and drove directly to a strip club, walked in and, by his command, got on stage. Dollars flew at her from the 10 or so patrons, and with each green spec the on-screen cash number increased. Then the husband called her. Yelling so loud that James had to turn down the volume. He grew angry. The reminder of what he was going through was not a welcome sight. He promptly dropped the phone, then smashed it with her shoe. Then, without hesitation she grabbed the closest patron and dragged him to the bathroom. As night rolled around, and the tiredness meter depleated, his day of nefarious behavior was over. As her car rolled into the driveway the husband ran out of the house. Screaming. Ten minutes of fighting in the driveway ensued, as much as James commanded them to stop. Then, they moved into the house and the screaming grew even louder. Then she hit him. She walked out the door and drove off in the car. James threw the keyboard across the room. He had already made it 4 days, but every second seemed like an eternity and he gave into the stress. All he could scrape together was not nearly as much as he wanted, but he was far from sober. Then he went back to the computer. Rage. Rage was all he felt as he watched the wife come back into the house to find the husband sleeping on the couch. James commanded her to sleep, and took control of the man. He pulled a jerry can from the garage, the had him spill gallons of gas across the first floor. He ordered the man to stay in the house. He was done. The next morning James had woken up with his head against the monitor. "Fuck," he said aloud feeling the hangover. He walked to the chair where he used to spend almost every free moment and turned on the TV. Nothing good on at 8 in the morning except the news. His hear stopped as he switched to his local news channel. Paralyzed, totally unable to move, to breathe, to think, he blinked. It was still there. The screen read: Husband takes life in murder suicide arson in Aullville. Three familiar faces were presented below.

"Tonight we go live to Stonehenge where the first meeting with the creator of the universe will be taking place. Melissa is on the scene. Melissa, can you hear me?" "Ah yes Chuck hello. We're all very excited down here as you can imagine. We simply can not wait to meet the creator in the flesh." "Yes it seems like quite the buzz down there right now. As I understand you will be speaking to the head researcher at CERN, who has been leading this project ever since it's inception?" "Yes in fact here he is Chuck. How are you feeling right now?" "Very excited but also nervous." "That's understandable. Now walk us through what will be happening very shortly..." "As you can tell we are now in the lovely surroundings of Stonehenge, and in the middle of the area here, we have set up a computer. Now on this computer we've installed a version of Windows 98. When the shadows of Stonehenge align, we've been instructed to start up MSDOS and type in a set of commands that will trigger an opening in the fabric of space time. This will allow a messenger from the Creators to come through and communicate with us directly." "So you've been in contact with the Creators recently?" "Yes, they send us instructions in some foreign language. It takes months to decode what they're saying. It took us years to set up this meeting alone." "How will you communicate with them today?" "We're not quite sure. They said they will make provisions for us so we don't really know, beyond that. We just have to trust that they'll be able to figure it out." "What happens if it's a disaster, if you can't communicate?" "It would be a real disappointment. I guess we'd have to go back to the drawing board in a sense." "Okay I'll let you get to it. Looks like it's almost time." - Some time passes. The shadows slowly begin to inch into alignment. Thousands of people have gathered to witness the event. Government officials and military personnel from all over the world are present. The shadows align. The head scientist jumps onto the computer and starts typing. Twenty seconds pass and he stops typing. The computer seems to shut down. The computer disappears. A small black door appears in its place. A small man dressed in a purple pinstripe suit and a fedora steps through. He isn't more than 3-4 feet high but has a certain commanding presence about him. He has a face which is wise beyond its years, although he looks no older than 21. "Soooooo..." He speaks in a high mannered fashion. "It is you who summoned me?" The head scientist looks slightly confused "Yes, sir. Hello. You're the one we've been talking with?" "No, not me fool. I am but a messenger. I come here to deliver a message." "A message? We were under the pretence that this was to be a discussion." "No, no discussion here. Only a message. Those are my orders." "I must say this is rather disappointing, nonetheless, what is the message?" "The message reads: Dear Humans of Earth, The computer simulation known as Universe 3987x93 will be ending in forty-two days. Please record any evidence you have of source code material and hand it to the Messenger exactly one day before shut down. This is required for testing purposes so that future generations of LifeSim may be made more robust and bug-free. We thank you for your participation in this simulation and wish you all a safe and disaster-free extinction event. Yours truly, The Creators And that's all it says. I will be on my way now. Good day!" And with that the small man disappeared in a puff of smoke. No one on Earth knew whether it was real or not. Many said it was an elaborate hoax. Some said a Government conspiracy. The scientists didn't even know. But sure enough, forty-one days from then, the small man came back, demanding evidence. They gave it to him. And a day later, the universe simulation was shut down. The Creators decided to patch the simulation program, LifeSim, after that. Patch 1.61 added in deeper levels of quantum abstraction. No other species before the Humans had delved that deep into quantum mechanics. There were a few other simulation instances that had to be ended that day as well. In one instance a species had actually ventured into a black hole. Thereby breaking the universe simulation. Despite these few setbacks the LifeSim program had been wildly successful and continued to show promise. Perhaps with a few more years of testing it will be ready for release. However there's one thing that the team needed to add more of, according to a message sent by the head of the Creators himself. A message which urged for more DLC and micro-transactions. A message which was signed; Andrew Wilson. Electronic Arts, CEO
