Maybe I tried to mumble something, but blood kept bubbling out of my mouth. And then, I was awake again. My wife was standing by my side, crying. She was holding my hand with her strangely warm hands. A gang of doctors and nurses surrounded me, talking about something. I was too confused to pay attention. How did I get here? Why can't I feel anything? Oh God, was I paralyzed? "I'm sorry, Mrs. Miller. he's passed away. There was nothing we could do, it was a terrible accident." What? That one single word screamed through my mind as my wife started bawling and nurses began moving out of the room. I tried to move. Couldn't even wiggle a toe. Or blink. Or breathe. The next few days were spent in a blur. All I could was think, and not very well. I drifted in and out of consciousnesses, always coming back dazed. It made no sense. How could I still be thinking when I was a corpse? At the funeral, I saw my parents, my wife and her parents, some of our friends..... it made me incredibly sad and I wanted to hug them and say goodbye. But how could I feel sad - or feel anything? I had no hormones or blood or spinal fluid. What held my thoughts? Maybe those left-field physicists were on the right track, I mused. Maybe it's a quantum thing. Or something. There was a small thud as my coffin bumped the bottom of the hole. Someone closed the lid, and I could feel the world get heavier as dirt covered the top. Very soon, the sounds all stopped, and I could see nothing. Too dark. I panicked for a moment, thinking I would go crazy to exist like this, but the thought melted away as I drifted off. Soon (poor word choice, really. I had no idea how much time had passed), I began to sense again. I saw the worms and beetles enter my coffin through little holes they had bored. I could hear their little hearts beating fast as they crawled over and inside me. Hell, I could feel the flesh ooze off my bones. I had no idea how. Actually, I was more amazed at how nonchalant it all seemed. I actually felt sort of cheerful whenever I drifted back into consciousness and felt little teeth pulling at sinew. Bizarre. Eventually, I began to talk with all the little critters - but not just them. The dirt and rocks and gases, too. OK, maybe talking isn't quite the word I'm looking for. More like..... feeling them. Understanding them. It's hard to explain, but everything seemed to have their own form of consciousness. Like a spirit or a soul, for lack of a better word. And as my body decayed to bone, I sort of began to tune in with all of my new "friends" down six feet under. One bright spring day (nah, I'm kidding, I have no idea what season it was) I knew it was almost over. I rarely got the chance to think anymore, mostly spending my "time" in a weird, dreaming state. But I knew this was the last time I would get to think. I concentrated on all my senses, and felt the world all at once. It was kind of beautiful. I know, that's pretty cliche. But there was no other word for it. I felt so at peace. I was becoming something else, something greater than my old single human self. I missed my family and friends, but not too much. After all, I would see them all again, someday. We will meet again when we were all one and the same. The thought of that gave me great pleasure and for the last time, I slipped away into the Earth.

[ Part 1 ] "Beep beep beep." I woke up with a start. Clearly someone had replaced my alarm clock and it's wrenching buzzing sound. Frankly, however, I was glad: the gentle beeping seemed to rise and fall to wake me up in the most gentile way possible. I made a mental note to talk to my roommate. Then forgot the mental note as I looked around the room. It wasn't just the alarm clock that had changed. The entire room had changed; the bed was clearly softer but somehow firmer where I needed it. The room itself was in shades of blue; a calming color which somehow made waking up easier. A dresser sat in the corner with my clothes laid out. In the adjacent bathroom, I heard the shower automatically turn on. After taking my shower and getting dressed, I could smell the smell of breakfast and I followed it to a small apartment-sized dining room. It had been neatly laid out: oatmeal with a touch of brown sugar and some fruit slices, and a couple of strips of what smelled like bacon but what looked like some sort of turkey substitute. If I had died and gone to heaven, I thought, then I'd need to talk to God about the food. Because breakfast without two eggs and a side of pork sausage and coffee? Nope. As I finished my bacon strips (which didn't taste all that bad, considering), I heard a knock on the door. "Come in." Inside my room stepped a man and a woman. Both appeared to be wearing white coats, and one carried a clipboard, scribbling notes. The woman asked, "How are you feeling?" "Where the hell am I?" Another room, painted white. A mirror on one wall, but I could see the faint glow of a couple of lights; clearly the mirror was one-way. Cameras were in the corner; if it weren't for the comfortable chairs, tastefully appointed table and a small fireplace giving the appearance of a living room, I'd swear it was a police interrogation room. Across from me three people sat; the woman from this morning, and two others; another man and woman, one typing into what looked like a small tablet computer. The man started: "I wish to apologize for what is happing to you. Approximately once a month we select a subject from the alternate Earth in order to serve as a sociological control when making decisions for governing our world. If you like, we have prepared a short video on the tablet next to you (gesturing to the table next to my chair, on which looked like a much thinner iPad Pro), which will help explain much of what is going on." The video seemed narrated by the same guy who voiced Darth Vader. He explained that in the late 1400's, the House of Plantagenet united determined to bring about a better world. The War of the Roses never took place; instead, the Renaissance was spurred on as the rulers of Europe turned to the wisest advisors they could find to help them make better laws. These scientists, mathematicians and philosophers helped to provide a framework which led the entire world to a new era, one where people are healthy, happy and live in peace and harmony. To bolster these points, images of clean cities crowned with tall, white smooth buildings slid cleanly by. There were no cars; instead, the cities appeared to be designed around a walkable inner core, and mass transit points leading to other cities and to countryside parks and manufacturing facilities. The air seemed clean, the clouds puffy and white, and the video concluded with faces of smiling, happy, multiculturally balanced array of people, all seemingly happy and healthy. The video ended. "I'm impressed," I responded at the end of the video. "So let us start with the questions," one of the women asked. She held up her own tablet, and an array of pleasing pastel colors showed on the screen. "Which color makes you feel productive?" "Sorry?" "If you found yourself in an office cubical, which one of these colors would make you feel more productive?" "I still don't understand the question." "That's okay, we'll come back to that question." Swipes finger on tablet, another array of color choices comes up, deeper and ranging from black to dark rich reds and blues. "If you were buying a bicycle, which color would you choose?" "Wait, why are you asking me?" "Because we wish to compare your choices against test subjects from our own world, in order to draw a correlation between color choices and their ability to satisfy emotional needs." "Why don't you ask the people who live here? Why not give them a choice?" The man, who had been watching our exchange, frowned. "Choice is irrelevant." "What?" "We have achieved our high level of peace and wealth by the scientific method, not through the chaos of the marketplace of individual choice." I stared at the man across from me, dumbfounded. I was staring at the floor in my well-appointed interrogation room. After a long pause I slowly looked up. "Why do you say that choice is irrelevant?" "Just that," the man smiled. "We found long ago that if left to the people's own devices, the long array of small choices they make often lead to larger choices. It's what you would call the'butterfly effect'; one person's discontent with the size of his room leads to a group of people expressing discontent over some other imagined failure and that eventually leads to groups of people rebelling, which eventually leads to war." He leaned forward to drive his point home. "We know, for example, the series of wars your people fought over the past 500 years: the genocides, the exterminations. We have largely avoided these failures, the extinction of the Native Americans on your home continent, the pogroms against the Jews, Armenians and Gypsies in your Europe. And we've done this through the careful scientific study of people, to limit choice to those things we have proven to maximize happiness, health and productivity. "Take, for example, our cities. We have determined that the best way to organize our cities is by increasing the walkability score of most neighborhood zones, to allow people to travel effortlessly to the restaurants or entertainment centers of their choice without having to use the self-propelled gasoline-powered engines of your world which are now choking your air, or the horse drawn carts which polluted your streets." I stopped him. "How do you know so much about my world." "Centuries ago, an accidental discovery allowed us to open a portal to your world. Since then we have been observing how your people live, borrowing inventions from your world and expanding upon them, perfecting them to allow us to improve the health of our own citizenship." "Wait, why do you need to borrow inventions from our own world? If you are lead by the smartest mathematicians and scientists of your world, why do you have to borrow inventions from ours?" The man shifted uncomfortably in his chair. "This has been the subject of a century-long research project. It's part of the reason why you are here." "I don't understand." "Our scientists don't understand why technological advances take place in your world but not in ours at the same pace. It's something we've been studying for a century, and it led us to pull people from your world as control subjects to figure out why there are gaps in productivity."

Jacob made his way through the massive crowd that had swarmed the walls of the restaurant. They were all gathered around a single table, and near the table was his date for the night. She sat there, in her white cocktail dress, holding a bottle of red wine in one hand and gripping a fat man's arm in her other. He was on the floor, moaning in pain with his face buried into the crumb covered surface. "Please let me go. I'm sorry. I won't do that again." Jacob's date, Veronica, made a small twitch of the arm and there was a slight snap. The man began to bellow in pain. Veronica smiled and spoke with a voice that had hints of sexuality and just a dash of anger. "Sorry for what?" The man was wiggling on the floor, trying to escape her grasp, then yelled out "I'm sorry for slapping your ass." With those words she let him be off and he ran away like a sweat covered baby fearing for his life. Commotion died down and people began to clear back to their seats. Veronica spotted him among the thinning crowd. "Jacob!" she exclaimed "I'm so happy to see you. Please, sit down" Jacob hardened the grip that he had on the flowers and swallowed back the ball that had built in his throat. He sat down, his eyes filled with wonder at the woman sitting before him. Her biceps seemed much larger, her hair was a mess, and he thought he saw a tattoo on her back. He didn't want to bring any of it up though, he simply sat there holding the flowers. Veronica snapped at them with her hands and pressed them against her face "mmmm these smell so nice, I can't remember how long it's been since I've been able to enjoy the scent of roses. Thank you Jacob." Jacob smiled, slid back in his chair and tried to think of things to say as his brain tried to figure out a logical conclusion as to how she was able to flip a three hundred pound man. Luckily, she was really busy chugging the bottle of wine to worry about his awkward stammering. The waiter passed by and Veronica grabbed onto his waist cloth. "How much longer on the food?" she inquired intensely. The waiter was a bit nervous to answer "Yes miss, the food should be here soon, it's simply a large order. Once again we apologize for that rude customer just now. She slapped the waiter on the back and let out a joyous laugh "No worries my man, I'm just starving, that's all." Jacob slowly raised his voice "Y-you ordered already?" Veronica smiled "Yes! Don't worry, there will be plenty for the both of us!" Jacob rubbed the back of his head, hoping some genie of clever things to say would emerge, but all he could amount to speak was "What have you been up to?" Her eyes lit up, her face was strewn into a wide grin, as she was about to explode in conversation she placed a single finger over her lips and blushed a little "I would love to tell you. But it's a long story." "It's been three years. A lot can happen in three years." Veronica leaned back and placed her bare feet on the table "You have no idea." Before Jacob could respond, three waiters came out. Each hand was filled with several plates, and they placed them one by one onto their table. By the end of it looked as if they were hosting a buffet. Veronica waited for the last plate to be set down and instantly she began to scarf it all down. One hand filled itself with a biscuit, the other grabbed the shrimp. Her teeth were working on a steak while her fingers wrapped themselves around a juicy slice of ham. Her lips suckled down bowl after bowl of soup and any room that could have been used for conversation was instead given to her hulking appetite. Veronica was three plates in and Jacob had barely finished his grilled salmon. The mood was off, he felt a little unsure of it all, and after watching the date slowly fall apart he pulled out a 100 dollar bill, left it at the table to pay the bill, and then slowly left. Food still in her mouth, she spoke up "Jawcob. Whats wong?" He smiled politely and then scratched at the back of his head again "Sorry, but things don't seem to be working out. I hope you can find somebody you're a bit interested in." As he was leaving his feet stopped at the sound of Veronica's fist smashing at the table. He turned and saw her standing there with her long wild hair flowing in the sudden wind that had appeared to assist her in a moment of pure badass fixation. "Jacob, you are staying. For three years I have been waiting to get back to Earth. For three years I have been stuck at the other edge of our universe. For three years I have fought a battle that was not mine. For three years I dug myself to freedom and did unspeakable things for the sake of democracy on a world that was not home to my kin. And now, after three years, after three years of waiting, and reading your text over and over again, I have a chance to get back here, and go out on a date with a really nice guy, and halfway through he stands up and walks away from it? I don't think so mister. Sit down." The restaurant was silent. Jacob sat down. Veronica sat down. She smiled. She blushed. "Sorry for the outburst. And I'm sorry for the eating, and the smelling of the flowers and my overall attitude. I'm just really happy to see you finally. I really like you Jacob." He smiled "I like you too." Veronica began to eat in a more calm manner, the music returned to the building and her lips danced around the wind glass. "So Jacob, do you know why I never called you back that night?" "Honestly, no." Her grin returned, "Then, please, allow me to explain."

There must have been something in the cold air that hit me as I stepped out of the shower. Without even thinking, I reached for the beer I had left waiting on the counter. It had been 15 minutes since my last drink- I was becoming much too lucid. I brought the bottle to my lips, and then I glanced into the mirror. All of a sudden it hit me. All of the shrinks, the meds, the depression and anguish of the past few years flew through my head as I stared at myself. In a beautifully jarring moment of clarity, it finally all made sense. All of this wasn't my parents' fault. It wasn't my teachers, my exes, my past, society, or any other bullshit scapegoat I had ever thought of. It was me. I wasn't some lost soul as I liked to think. I wasn't doomed to a life of mediocrity by some vengeful god or unfortunate twist of fate. I knew damn well what I needed to do. I just needed to do it. I put down the beer. I poured myself a glass of water. The next morning, I signed up for a gym membership and applied to the local college to finish my degree. I finally realized I was sick of leading the life I thought I was supposed to lead. It's my goddamn life, and I'm going to make it exactly what I want. Success is success, and failure is a learning experience. My only regret is that I didn't realize all of this sooner.

" Sir? It's almost time to begin. " I glanced up from my desk, strewn with reports from my generals. Pushing the button on my intercom, I replied " Thank you, Alonso. I'll be right down. " I put down the paper I was holding and smiled. The last remnants of the American Empire's army had been crushed, and with their demise came the death of the last remaining free nation. It was done. I had become the first man to ever achieve total world domination. And there was something that had to be done. Stepping into the foyer of my palace, I saw Alonso tapping his foot, waiting for me by the door. Alonso was my right-hand man. We had known each other for years, and I trusted him with much more than just my life. He was the chief of my military, and he used to handle foreign affairs back when there were still foreign countries with whom affairs were managed. " Ready for your big speech, sir? " Alonso was beaming. " You've been looking forwards to this moment for years. How do you feel? " " Just great. A little nervous, I suppose. I told you not to call me " sir ," Alonso. " " Sorry, sir. Er, sorry, Max. Well, have you got your speech? " " Don't worry, I won't need one. How do I look? " " Amazing. Wonderful choice of suit, may I add. " " Good, I want to look great for the crowd. Here, let's go. " The crowd outside the Palace, which had been at a dull roar before, burst into a frenzy as I opened the doors and walked out from under the veranda. As I strode towards my golden podium, two guards quickly hurried to my sides. Despite my overwhelming support in these parts, there was still the odd assassin I had to contend with. Alonso and the guards stopped just before the podium and took up their positions. This was it. My moment of glory. This moment would be honored in history books long after my death. I will have finally achieved what I set out to do nearly thirty years ago. I glanced back at Alonso, and he gave me a thumbs up. Feeling my anxiety harden into my usual iron resolve, I gave him a pursed smile, wiped my brow, and stepped up to a hail of cheers, waving signs, and camera flashes. " Greeting, ladies and gentlemen. I have come to you, noble people of the Great Republic, with grand news. Our armies have defeated the insolent Imperials, and established our message of prosperity and unity across the entire globe! The sun shall never set on our glorious nation! " At these words, the crowds only applauded louder. The clicking of cameras was nearly deafening now. I smiled and raised my arms in victory. Then, I put on a solemn face and continued. " However, that is not all. I have an important announcement to make. As of today, I am stepping down from my role of Imperator of the Great Republic " The cheering stopped. Silence fell. Even the reporters packed around my stand stopped taking pictures to gape at me. Then, the whispers started. The Imperator of the entire planet was simply stepping down? Impossible! Something's wrong. He's sick, he's ill! But no. I'd never felt better in my entire life. " Yes. Today, I will resign from my position. I will no longer be your glorious leader. As my replacement, I shall appoint my head general, Sir Alonso Shafi. " I looked back at Alonso. His eyes were wide, and he looked at me with his mouth wide open. As I gave him a small smile, he mouthed: What the fuck? I turned back to the roiling masses, now on the brink of rioting. I wasn't done. There was still one thing left. " But! But, but, but! Before I do so, I shall make my first, last, and only decree as Imperator. " Every man, woman, and child on the planet waited with bated breath for my next words. I liked the feeling of control, but that wasn't what I was looking for. That wasn't what I needed. " Let this law forever stand in the halls of time. Let it be known, here and now, that any man who, from this moment forwards, pronounces " gif " as " jif " shall be executed immediately. There shall be no exceptions, just as justice must be done swiftly and without hesitation. " Again, silence. This time, there was no whispering. " That is all. Thank you, and have a productive day. Glory to the Republic! " As the people of the Great Republic exploded into shouts and cries, I turned and stepped down from my podium. I had finally set things straight. The goal I had set out to achieve so many years ago had been realized. I had righted a wrong, and all the deaths I had caused as my armies conquered the globe was a small price to pay for the sins of a generation. As the new Imperator of the Great Republic turned around to scream my name, I slowly lowered a pair of shades over my eyes. It was done.

This is a forbidding planet, full of hostile wildlife, a scorching climate, and uncertain vegetation. I have already scanned through my gifted supplies, boons from my family and friends to aid in my survival through my trial. Though meager, as is customary, I believe they will be enough to get me started here. Hunting and gathering tools, some strong rope, and a few fire stones to ward off the chill. My first nights here will not claim my life. In truth I do not fear for my ability to survive on this feral world at all, my clan has always been hardy and strong and I am no exception. My concern lies with the true reason for our kind's forced exile: Communion. My psychic sense have always been... subpar at best, and my father has made no bones about his worry that I will turn out like my brothers, a fierce warrior but unsuited for leadership. He has ruled for 120 cycles and is beginning to show his age, by the time I am allowed to return it will nearly be time for his sending. I desperately wish to make him proud, and allow him to safely pass to the next plane. I have read the guides given to me by our shamans, on the nature of Communion and how to encourage it. I can clear my mind of thought in a heartbeat, and my physical sense are unparalleled amongst my kin. Preparing for contact is a simple thing, I simply can not figure out how to extend my mind in greeting to another being's. Perhaps my time on this world will fix that, forcing me to live on wits and instinct will bring me closer to the creatures here, hopefully enough that I might establish Communion with one of them. I also hope that my will proves strong enough to endure the bear of a feral mind, what few connections I have made with my kind have been intense as is, and that is with both minds having received training. I have heard too many tales of gifted upstarts mentally linking with large and fearsome beasts, only to have their minds brushed aside and dominated by them. Only time will tell, and time is something I have plenty of. For now I will focus on survival, and possibly even comfort should this planet relinquish its secrets to me quickly. I hear a faint howling on the winds, and soon I will see if I am to be a hunter or prey on this planet. It is time. I have weathered the harsh environment of this planet for two decades and have emerged its master. Though nothing here can speak the creatures know this planet as Carnor, and I have learned all I can of this beautiful and savage world. I still remember the night of my first communion, after five long years of grueling seasons, vicious indigenous creatures, and dangerous fauna. A storm destroyed my camp, I was wounded after fighting a pack of four legged hunters, and I was locked in mortal struggle with the last beast left alive. We both bled from many wounds, our life forces dangerously close to ebbing away, and in my desperation I reached out to a mind that was as hurt and scared as mine. Communion. Our bond was... intense. I recall spending several days crawling around on all fours hunting with the beast, nursing our wounds and regaining our strength, before my mind returned to me. Abrecan became my best companion in the years to follow, showing me the way his kind hunts and gathers. I taught him what I could of logic and reason as well, and though he never developed the capacity for speech he certainly had the ability to display cunning. My next Communion was with a great two legged beast I call Brutus, after Abrecan and I found him wounded and abandoned by his pack. This Communion was different, an extended hand of mercy and care instead of a frantic gambit for survival. I learned why Communion is so important, and powerful, a skill for my people. It wasn't just my will that met with Brutus ', but Abrecan's too. The three of us shared the load of our minds connecting and we all were enhanced by it, learning of each others ways and customs. It was a feeling unlike anything I could even describe. Here I stand years later, Communed with nearly every creature I come across, linking this world's wildlife in a strong and secure web of understanding and trust. Hunters still hunt prey, but together we have forged new means of doing so. Creatures bred specifically without being communed, still acting on their base instincts to be hunted and eaten without having the burden of understanding placed on them. We work together to build shelter, cure the sick, and watch over our lands when rival packs wander in. Though I insisted we all remain equals, the creatures of this planet still treat me as Alpha to all, their protector and master, and I take my role extremely seriously. Ironically I came to this planet to learn to lead, so I might take my father's crown from him, and I find myself needing to designate an heir of my own. Abrecan has long since passed, but I have decided that Brutus shall take my place as Alpha here. He has mastered Communion alongside me, and understands the importance of the peace and connections we have forged. I look forward to returning soon, to see how Carnor has grown in my absence. It occurs that these thoughts and stories can be found throughout this diary I have kept, an epic ledger of my growth, adventures, and ultimately my ascension. But I suppose I am simply feeling nostalgic, knowing that this chapter of my life is at a close. I am ready to lead my people now, but I will never forget the savage world that made me who I am.

"You're not the person I knew you could be." Those were the final words that Tony heard from the Captain. And for the first time since the mess began, he was speechless. Although if you asked him, it was because he was too exhausted to say anything else. Not that Steve cared. He was done. Done with the fighting, done with Tony. His former friend and Ally showed him a part of himself that he didn't want to see. A side of him he didn't know he had. A darkside. Steve Rogers came too close to becoming the thing he hated that it scared him. He was a man out of time, one who's morals and ethics were at an odds with modern life. In a way, he was glad that he was back in the past, this way he could grow together with the nation, bit by bit. And since everything worked out, he didn't need to fight anymore. Not that he could if he wanted to. If would cause a mess to the timestream. At least that's what he heard. "So this is what quiet is like." Steve Rogers took in a deep breath of fresh, 1950's air. The home salesman nodded. "Well it is a good day in the neighborhood Mr...?" "Rogers." Steve smiled. "Mr. Rogers."

CFL was on her way home from work one day when she decided to pay her old friend WOH a visit, as she heard through the grapevine he was getting sick. She stopped at his apartment, and seeing his car outside was surprised when he didn't respond to her buzzer. Worried, she broke into the apartment being the crafty gal she was, and worked her way up to his floor. When she opened the door, she couldn't believe her own eyes. WOH sat dead, a bullet through his head. FL scampered around to find evidence, and as she fished her hand through the dark room, she chanced upon a gun. Suddenly, the sound of a gunshot pierced through the air. CFL nearly had a heart attack, but soon realized the sound was not authentic. Police sirens were quickly heard outside the apartment, and CFL, checking the fresh wound, realized she had just been framed.

When I heard the scream, I jumped a little. I waited a moment to see if there was more. There was only silence. I wondered to myself what had happened. Rubbing my eyes, I yawned and shivered a little. It was hard to tell where the sound had come from, but I was almost certain that it was the small house on the corner. It was a tiny street, and I doubted anyone would be awake at this hour. There was no-one around. I simply had to find out who screamed and why. Maybe an old lady fell over, and if I help her, my boss will be proud, and then I'll be in the papers for saving the elderly, and then maybe I can be a Cop like my Dad. I walked slowly through the garden that looked very neglected, full of weeds and plastic wrappers. I felt kinda cold. But, raising my chin a little, I strode up to the front door. I knocked 3 times and waited. Nothing happened. Peering through the window, I caught a glimpse of a man. He was sat cross legged on the floor. Looking around, the house looked pretty well furnished. The guy must have been rich. I tapped on the window. The man didn't move. I wasn't sure what to do at this point. Maybe the man just didn't want to be disturbed, and I should leave at once. But the scream I heard was definitely a woman. Just as I made a decision, I looked up at the movement inside. The man was gone. In panic, I ran behind the house and crouched behind some smelly bins. It smelt dreadful. I heard the front door open, then footsteps. They weren't coming in my direction so I crept to the edge of the building and peeked round. The man wasn't there. I stood up and began walking to the front door, which was wide open. Then I noticed the smell again. I looked down. I was standing in a pool of something nasty. I hopped out of it in disgust, and began to examine the interior. There was a grandfather clock that wasn't ticking, several rugs that looked extremely expensive, and many ornate paintings, statues and vases dotted around. It was strange for such a small house. I noticed a large barrel in the corner, and walked over to see what was inside. It was full of rings. There were hundreds of them in there, Gold, Silver- even a few diamond rings. I picked one up, and it read "Sarah McCollin and Peter McCollin." It was a wedding ring. I picked up another. "Emily Garther and Dick Garther, forever and forever." That was odd. All the wedding rings belonged to different people. There was another barrel in the other corner. I walked over to it and gasped. Now I understood the smell. Inside the barrel was a liquid that smelt like vinegar..... and Eyeballs. I felt dizzy and homesick and very scared all of a sudden. Someone had collected human eyeballs in their house. I froze. Someone was behind me. I spun around, and I looked up at the man I had seen before. There was something wrong with this man. He didn't look ugly, he just didn't look human. His head was too tall and thin, his eyes looked like those of a lizard, and his breath smelt of rot. I didn't say anything and neither did he it. There was a moment when I looked at the thing dead in the eye and I could feel something..... It wasn't pain or sadness or happiness or excitement..... I felt hopeless. I felt like I could just shrivel up and die right there. To this day. I will not forget that feeling. What happened next was not exciting or incredible. I walked past the thing and left the house, shutting the door behind me. Then I ran through the weedy garden, down the tiny street and I didn't stop running until I got to the police station. I told them that there was a scary man who had eyeballs in his house and I gave them the address. Two Cops went to check it out and I waited in the Police Station and the Police gave me a glass of milk. Only one Cop came back. They called the FBI and told me to go home. I went home. It was in the papers the next day, with the headline'Jack the Ripper returns'. That was a lie, he wasn't Jack the Ripper. And my name wasn't in the story either, which sucked. My buddy thinks he was an alien. I reckon he was just a loser with a weird hobby. The house and the smelly bins and the weedy garden are all gone now. It was blown up. The whole town got to watch. It was great. I think the man is dead now. At least, I would imagine so, with his house blown up and all those Cop's bullets in his head. Dan slammed a fist down on the table, "So. Damn. Close." "Okay Dan, calm down and tell me about it," Steve was another scientist working at the DOD labs. His work was on a Gigawatt Death Ray. "Think about it Steve, a million minds all like ours, synthesized in a matter of hours! One thousand you's with the exact same mental makeup and ability. I just can't solve the power problem!" The other scientist gave him a strange look, "Just wait until 7pm. The buildings power usage decreases when all the other scientists stop working for the day. You can allocate the extra power." "That will work! That will fix it! Why are you looking at me like that?" "Dan, I've told you how to solve that problem two days in a row now." "Sorry, I must be getting tired. Unfortunately, I can't try that solution until tomorrow because the cloning room needs time to sterilize itself after I leave and..... Oh shit."

The two lab-coated scientists stared into the central containment tank. Suspended in the center was an amorphous blob wreathed in a tangle of multicolored wires. The thing pulsed slowly, breathing the green tinted water. The tentacles of the creature hung limply, drifting slowly with the soft current of the tank filtration unit. Tap, tap, tap, "How's our little octo-bot doing today?" The tentacles twitched, but even the creatures eyes remained stationary. "You think it's dying, Ted?" Ted continued to stare into the tank, "We're all dying, dude. Yeah, I know what you mean though. It's obviously not dead-dead though." He nodded his head towards the nearby wall of monitoring equipment. There were a dozen square meters of various displays, graphs, and other metrics commonly associated with life signs. The two stood in silence for a few moments more. Ted cleared his throat and stretched his arms, "Whatever. Did you finish the notes?" James, the taller of the two scientists, answered in a stereotypical scientist voice, "Year 42 Day 238: Subject shows no signs of change. Vitals stable. Observation continuing." He laughed and continued in his normal voice, "I bet I could write a little program that would just update the date and write these silly notes for me. Wouldn't even have to show up to the lab! It's not like anything ever changes. Ol' Blobbly..... Just hangin' out." Ted tried to sound outraged, "Dude! " , but laughed, "Don't say that shit man. What would the professor think?" "He'd probably say,'James Thornton! Science is not built on shortcuts and time savers. Science is built on the foundations of blah blah blahology. Ted held a hand to his chin, mocking the way their professor tended to stand. In the exaggerated voice of an old man he spoke, "Indeed!" The scientists chuckled as they walked out the heavy steel door, triggering the magnetic lock on their way out. Later that evening, Ted was on his fourth beer when he experienced that stunning shock that people tend to experience when they've forgotten something important for way too long. "I'll be right back, dudes..... I forgot something." The small group in his living room barely even acknowledged him over the hubbub of the story being told by James. Ted rushed into his bedroom and woke up his personal computer. He grumbled to himself, " ..... can't believe I forgot the damn, stupid, damn biometric recorder. God damn the damn..." He quickly typed in the username and password that would allow him to remote-in to the laboratory computer. He moved some windows around as he did a habitual cursory overview of the various monitoring equipment. Everything appeared to be nominal. There were no notable changes in the records for the last hour at least. He minimized all windows except for the primary monitoring nexus software, but stopped and stared when he noticed the footage from the persistent webcam that ran in the background of the lab computer. Even in the dark the glow from the myriad monitors allowed him to see that the primary containment tank was empty. He mumbled to himself, "What the..." Ted attempted to increase the bandwidth and quality of the camera, hoping that maybe this was some sort of graphical artifact or glitch. The image clarified further, losing most of the blockiness, but still the tank appeared to be empty. The increase in resolution allowed him to note the harness that usually held the specimen hanging empty from the top of the tank. He squinted as he panned the shoddy camera around the room. It was a cheap cam from the electronics store and not designed to pan very much. As the camera drifted slowly towards the edge of the desk he thought he saw movement. He attempted to pan further, but the camera would not move in that direction. He panned downwards instead. He noticed that the keyboard was nearly falling off the edge of the desk at a strange angle. "There is no way..." Ted could practically see the desk of earlier this afternoon in his mind. The two scientists never left the lab messy. He clicked once to allow the camera to pan back to the default position. He sat back in his chair he absently watched the camera move. He could hear the party continuing in his absence outside. The camera had reverted to default position. Ted could clearly see that the tank was once again occupied. Squinting, he brought his face close to his monitor. "What the hell, man?" He hissed, "Glitches." He double checked that the biometrics were now being recorded. Only one hour of data is automatically saved without the record feature. He took a moment to look closely at this older data. The signs showed that the creature must have been in the tank the whole time. It must have been a camera glitch. He sighed loudly, "I'm going crazy." Scientist instincts took over and he decided to troubleshoot the camera issues before he went back to the party outside. Unthinking, he simply opened the browser of the lab computer and began to type. How to fix webcam [ Search ] Ted paused for a moment. What did the autofill say? He hit the back button and typed his request again, slowly this time. H. Ho. How [ human think ] The hell? He clicked a few times to open the history. Dozens of pages had been visited today, but only one had been accessed during their work hours. He browsed through the entries, mostly search queries: how human think, why human speech, human speak how, can think, human brain think, what blobby, james thornton human name, james thornton human purpose. Most of these searches were performed in the last few hours. Ted noted that the most recent query was 15 minutes ago - A wikipedia article for human anatomy. He paused for a moment before standing slowly and walking back towards the party. James looked up from the drinking game on the coffee table, "Hey man, your turn..... Fuck, dude, you alright?" "James. We..... Everyone needs to go. We need to go to the lab." His friend laughed, but looked weirded out, "Nah, man. Drinky time, not worky time." Ted still looked stunned, "No, James. Call the professor, we need to go to the lab immediately. Something is happening at the lab. The specimen. I think it's awake."

The night was quite dark and the stars shone quite brightly, Tim lay awake, as he did nightly, His family, you see, were so boring and grim, But Tim had a plan to do them all in. nbsp; Every morning and night, between five and eight, He's slip out the door and then through the front gate, And syphon some fuel from his fathers car, He needed a lot, for he had to go far. nbsp; His plan was quite bold, maybe even insane, But he'd rather be dead than listen again, To his fathers complaining and his mothers nagging, He'd tried to be good, but his patience was flagging. nbsp; He needed a plan that could go unsuspected, And once it had started could not be corrected, So he planned it all out for one night in June, He'd fire a rocket and bring down the moon. nbsp; Tim was quite smart, and was up for the task, Though collecting the bits was quite a big ask, He managed to get the rocket and fuel, And assembled the parts when he came home from school. nbsp; At last the night came and he slipped out the door, Away from his dad, who he could hear snore, The rocket was ready - he lit the engines and ran, And hid in the bushes, as was the plan. nbsp; The rocket soared up and into the sky, It burned red, then white and began to get high, And finally hit on the very moon's top, It hit good and hard but it still didn't stop, nbsp; The rocket burned on and to Tim's delight, It started to push the moon down from its height, It plummeted now, quickly falling to earth, While Tim did a dance and cried out with mirth. nbsp; For a long time it fell, but at last it drew near, Tim opened his arms, the ending was clear. It would squish down his house with the greatest of ease..... But what bounced off the roof was a large block of cheese. nbsp; Tim looked at the cheese with his rocket embedded, His mission had failed, his dreams had been shredded. So he picked up the rocket and munched on the cheese, Tomorrow he'd see about dying with bees.

Riding above the setting sun came a man atop a large ashen horse. The animal bore the weight of its master as well as several sacks of food, ale, and the mans weapon, shield, and armor. A large linden round shield adorned the riders back; its once brightly painted sigil of a raging direwolf now faded after years of use. Sword and ax straddled his side and his bow and arrows were safely stored in one of his packs. Coming up on a grassy knoll, he could see the landmark he had been riding for; the Black Dragons Den. Once a great keep built along a now crumbling wall bordering two ancient kingdoms, the infamous Black Dragon had taken up residence in its abandoned walls in recent times. Everyone knew of the monstrosities that the dragon inflicted upon mankind whenever it left its lair. The beast was privy to setting entire villages aflame, consuming whole herds of farm animals, and, more recently, kidnapping King Cyneric's daughter; Primula. Nearly a year ago, the black dragon flew into Dagenham and wreaked havoc upon the inhabitants. The city's garrison did the best they could to fell the monster, but ultimately their efforts were fruitless. The dragon razed half the city to the ground, gorged itself on hundreds of people, and eventually flew for the kings keep. The beast tore through the castle walls after some effort, entered the castle walls, clutched the princess in it's nasty claws, and then proceeded to fly back to its lair. In the aftermath of the dragons debauchery, the king spared no expense at trying to rescue his daughter. He raised his entire personal levy as well as those of his vassals and rode for the dragons lair. They were quickly slaughtered upon arrival. King Cyneric and few hundred men managed to escape the dragons wrath, but the rest weren't as fortunate. Upon arriving back home safe and sound, the king immediately began drafting any able bodied man in his kingdom to take up arms and march for the dragons lair with an incentive of unfathomable riches and marriage to his daughter for whoever slayed the beast. Despite this, only a few thousand answered his call. Nevertheless, the king once again went off to deal with the beast. Once again he was beaten handily. This time, however, he returned to Dagenham with a charred backside and but a few dozen men. With no one willing to answer his call for a third march on the dragons lair, King Cyneric was left with little choice but to turn to men of hire. That's where Sigeberht came in. Now descending the lowly hill, Sigeberht mounted off his horse and set up camp in the cover of some thick foliage. He would rest for the night before engaging the beast come dawn. "Sigeberht, your exploits are legendary. From here to the walls of Anaheim tales of your adventures are known to every man, woman, and child. They say even the birds sing of your deeds. You're a living legend. There is no man alive as skilled as you." "You honor me, your majesty," Sigeberht began. "But while my deeds be mighty and my skills unmatched, I do none of it for free." Cyneric chuckled aloud at that. "That is true. It is also known to every man, woman, and child that you are a man of coin first and foremost. If the pay isn't right, you won't even consider doing the job." "Aye," Sigeberht responded. "So what're you offering me to rescue your daughter?" "I offer you nobility. And with nobility all the perks that go with it. You'll be elevated to the highest title possible without giving you my crown. That is the title of Duke. I'll provide you with a fetching noblewoman of prestige to marry and endow you with enough wealth for you to retire from the lifestyle you currently live. What say you, Sigeberht? Will you rescue my daughter from the clutches of the vile beast?" "Make that fetching noblewoman your daughter and we have a deal." The king was taken aback by the high demand. "I offer you luxury of the world and yet you still ask for the heavens above! I have but one child. That is my dearest Primula. Whoever weds her will be wedding into royalty. And you aren't of noble stock." "Then I guess your daughter is doomed," Sigeberht said as he began to walk away. "Have fun dealing with the dragon. Maybe he'll marry her and be your new son-in-law." "Wait," yelled the king just as Sigeberht was making for the exit. "I yield. There is no one more suit for the task than you. I can't afford not to hire you. You will wed my Primula as a just reward for her rescue." "Good," he spoke aloud before exiting. Sigeberht awoke from his slumber with an inaudible yawn. Rising to his full height, he unpacked his arms and armor and began to gear up. A simple steel helmet adorned his head. Lamelar armor draped over a suit of chain mail dressed his body. Sword and ax were sheated on his side, bow and arrows lined his back, and his round shield was held firmly by his left hand. Once he was fully geared, he ate a simple meal of salted rabbit and ale before praying to the Allfather. Kneeling on one knee, Sigeberht closed his eyes and raised his arms at full length above his head. Whispering a simple prayer, he didn't spend too much time before rising up and heading for the beasts lair. Will finish this up later. Have to jet off to work right now.

"I haven't been planetside in ages," John shouted over the roar of re-entry. "This is the third time this year I've stood on real dirt." Brian lifted his head, finally waking up. Our ship was little larger than a capsule, big enough for just the three of us. They told us the heat shield was tough, but for some reason I couldn't shake the feeling the millimeter-thick ceramics were going to fail. We rocked around in the air like a skipping stone. "How's our descent looking?" I asked, failing to take my mind off the heat shields. "One hundred kilometers and dropping, we should hit the clouds soon." John brought up visual. Flames licked the camera, translating to streaks of bright colors on screen. After a few minutes, the flames died a bit, revealing the dead planet. "What kind of god..." Have you ever seen your home after a big fire? How the wreckage still smolders for days? Each one of us felt something deep down, some recognition of our ancestral home. We weren't ready to see the truth first hand. That the world was still burning.

He sat across the street from her house, making sure he had all the necessary supplies for the night. Susan Burbank, late twenties, red hair, just like the 23 others before her. He suppressed a grin, humming quietly as he worked, reminiscing over all that had happened these past several months. The first months of his new life, his real life. He stopped fighting the urge to smile. He could see her through the brightly-lit kitchen window, busying herself with something at the stove, serene and blissfully ignorant of her fate. She had just recently moved to Danby, the little town in the corner of Vermont that he called home. Guessing from the plethora of blockbuster thriller posters, t-shirts, and other knick knacks littering the house, she'd most likely heard of this place through all the recent coverage surrounding his exploits. A fan of his work - the media would have a field day. Not that they weren't enjoying themselves already. Always one to play with his food, the sensationalism and drama of the crimes was his favorite part, and he continuously tried to up the ante. There were a few things he always kept the same, calling cards of sorts - his victims were all young, red-headed women, all residents of Danby, and at each crime scene he left something red, just out of place enough for people to catch on. Within these parameters, he tried to get creative. One woman he left diced up in her bathtub, filled to the brim with tomato sauce. He painted all of one victim's walls bright red, her body in a red dress to match. His personal favorite was the time he'd sewn into the girl's stomach a bright red cellphone. The scream of the maid that found her when he called it coud've been heard miles away. The headlines were splattered with every pun and nickname imaginable; "The Crimson Killer," "Added Red-Head Dead," "Slaying in Scarlet." The soon-to-be ghost town came alive again; places stopped closing and old places reopened, friends moved back in and people stopped talking about moving away, folks could finally rest easy without having to worry about the impending economic collapse. Nor would they ever have to from now on. After this, no one would ever forget Danby ever again. And they would never forget him. Almost time. Like clockwork, Susan appeared on the front step, ready for her nighttime jog. He pulled his mask from the duffel bag. It looked mostly human, but was just different enough to be something "else" and incredibly unsettling. A strange man coming at you was scary enough, but he'd found that what scared people most was what they didn't understand. Not only did the mask help hide his identity, but it created the illusion that he was not human at all but something unknown, even supernatural. Even better, he'd allowed the police to catch a few shots of him with the thing on near some of the crime scenes, so that when his victims spotted him all they knew was the horrible future that awaited them. All these factors helped add to the fear in his victims; their struggles, their screams, the fear in their eyes. That was the best part: the fear in their eyes. Following silently for a while, he positioned himself behind the girl at the end of a long, narrow, dimly lit street. He made a slight scraping sound with his shoe against the concrete, at just the right volume. The girl slowed and stiffened. After a heartbeat, she turned. And saw him. He started to run. With unlikely speed, Susan sprinted towards her house. This didn't bother him as he didn't plan on getting her in the street. What did bother him was the look on her face. That look. Or rather, the lack of it. The moment when they see him, that look of dawning realization, had been absent from her face, replaced by an undecipherable expression. Mildly troubled, he continued the pursuit, his worry quickly giving way to a fevered anticipation. As a fan of his work, Susan would be priviledged to something a little more elegant than the usual whore. He planned to completely empty her out and stuff her full of dark red rose petals, leaving more scattered throughout the house and yard. While she was still alive and screaming, of course. Susan reached her door and unlocked it after minimal fumbling with her keyring, slamming it behind her. Not that that made any difference, as he was going through the bathroom window. He wanted to make her feel helpless and hunted first. Make her feel afraid. He easily slid the window open, having unlocked and oiled it a few nights before, and slipped inside. Something immediately collided with his face, forcing his head to the ground. He briefly registers his own panicked confusion and the red-haired figure above him before the chloroform takes effect, and he blacks out. "Okay, open your eyes!" Trent Burbank did as he was told. His wife always loved planning surprises and giving gifts; he knew she had tried particularly hard for his birthday this year, and by the tone of her voice he guessed this gift was a big deal. He wasn't wrong. He let out a small gasp and a long low whistle. "I can't believe it, how did you get this?" She smiled, delighted at his reaction. "Honestly, I was expecting it to be a little more difficult." He laughed, shaking his head and pulling his wife in for a kiss. He gingerly takes the mask out of the box. "Let's go put this with the others. Where to next?"

I peer out through the darkness, Through the world I've always known. This is my home, my haven. It's all I've ever owned. And yes, it gets quite lonely, In solitude, I abide. But this is where I'm safe and sound, From the hurtful world outside. You know what the people say - Once bitten, and twice shy. I'll never let them hurt me now, They'll never see me cry. But unexpectedly, you appeared, Like an angel from above. You showed me truth and goodness, You taught me how to love. Even when the tears came down, You held me, close and tight. And when I fell, you carried me, Through my darkest nights. So in the end, because of you, I finally found my way. The path is clear, but there is just One thing I want to say: I don't know how I got here, Or how it came to be. But one thing that I'm sure of: Now, I'm finally free.

Day one was difficult, everyone around me did the exact same thing except for the players (who obviously played basketball). I'd randomly appear in a press room where people were asking Blake Griffin questions after each game. I had no choice but to join in with the reporters. I'd ask the same questions every night, "how is your offense clicking," "you guys are executing well, is this a sign of things to come" every day, every game. There's nothing to do but wait for the press conference and watch the game. I tried playing basketball one day, it took one charge from Anthony Davis to know that wasn't gon na happen. I've started messing with the game a bit, running out onto the court naked, stabbing the mascot. There's really nothing else to say, I have no way out, no way to enjoy where I am and no way to die. I'm stuck. Help me.

Writingthullu stares down at you with desdain. "A lurker for life? Always here for amusement from other people's work?" You have no idea what to say. All the good ideas always seem to flourish after you turn off your computer. And Writingthullu seems to be aware of this. "Don't give me that sad look! If you have a good idea, right it down on a piece of paper! Waiting for the next day never works. And what was that crap yesterday? You want to write but you cant even spell correctly! ITS DEITY, NOT DIETY! What was that supposed to be, a food god? If you dont know how to spell a word, just use a synonym like the rest of us. The word you were searching for is god." That wasnt helping. After 30 minutes of soul crushing insults, you confidence is pretty much shattered. "I'm giving you one last chance. Ill return in 2 hours. Make them count" A wave of relief swept through you as the door closed shut behind Writingthullu. The deadline was still there, but the absence of his overwhelming presence made it easier to think. Now you only needed to focus. "Hmm an army of horse sized ducks faces an army duck sized horses..... No, no, no. This is the same crap that shows up in WP everyday. I have to do something that doesnt sound like an Adam Sandler or Rob Schneider movie plot." You suddenly feel a surge of adrenaline as an invisible hand gently touches your shoulder. "You are not alone. We will help you." You let out a gasp and jump out of the chair as you begin to see a human shape take form before your eyes. "Who or what are you?" "Ghosts from the past. My name is Tolkien. Im sure you are familiar with some of my work. I have brought some friends" Various shapes take form and introduce themselves. Hello writer. Im Nabokov, nice to meet you. Phillip Pullman at your service" Another voice that sounded angry was being appeased by a woman. "Why am I here? Im not even dead!" "Oh quiet down, Murakami. This person needs our help. Im Jane Austen, dont mind him, he was just upset we interrupted his jazz listening session." One of them sounded confused. "Ok I dont think this is a dream, but it sure seems like one. Well, ill help out anyway I can. Stephen King at your service." You are still not sure what is happening, but an idea starts to form. Guided by some of the greatest storytellers, words pour violently from your brain into the paper. The 2 hour deadline is near completion. The various ghostly forms begin to say their farewells. Stephen King is slightly annoyed. "What? Wake up? No, I dont wan na. I'm having fun here, I want to see Writingthullu's reaction." All the forms slowly dissipate, with Murakami being the last. He lights a cigarrete, inhales deeply while staring at you. And then, after what seemed to be an eternity, exhales with a soft grin and whispers: "Good luck." His form completely fades afterwards. No more than 10 seconds after the forms fade out, Writingthullu burst through the door with a renewed evil smile on his face. You feel the hard prickle of fear on the back of your head and instinctively look down. As look down you see what you are holding in your hands. All thoughts of fear and doubt leave your mind, and that confidence is transmitted by the look in your eyes. Writingthullu looks at you puzzled. "You seem diferent. Did you manage to produce something interesting?" Without blinking or averting your eyes, you hand him the pages you finished typing a few minutes ago. "Why dont you find out by yourself?" As he starts reading, his face changes. He seems mesmerized, completely absorbed. When he finished reading his face turned to anger. You begin to feel scared once again. "Whats the matter? Is the story not pleasing?" He looks at you, his eyes fireballs of azure anger. "You were supposed to be the last one I needed to consume. My invasion of this realm would be complete after this. Never in my dreams I tought you capable of such a story. THIS WAS MY TIME! As he screams those words, a portal of some kind begins forming in the pages you handed to him. He fruitlessly tries to throw the pages on the ground, on the table, at you. Nothing seems to work. The portal grows and as the churning maelstrom begins to pull Writingthullu inside, he vociferates a final warning. "You wont be able to keep me locked forever. I will return and you wont be here to stop me." You smile and simply reply: "Probably not, but my work will endure. And I will inspire others. We will always be ready for you."

"You stop right there!" Michelle spun around in the entrance hallway and glared at her mother, who looked livid. "What?" "Don't'what' me," her mother said, holding up her phone. "I just got off the phone with the principal. He said - " "Yeah, yeah, I broke into his office. Big deal. It's just a prank." She turned toward the door as her mother screamed, "You're being suspended, you know? Your father was let go this morning; think of how high his blood pressure'll be after hearing about this. You stop there, you stupid girl. I said - " Her voice was silenced by the slamming door. Michelle strode down their driveway, pulling out a small pouch from her pocket as she went. "Hey, Mich," said Ellis, who had been leaning on the letterbox. He pulled her in for a kiss, but she held him back. "Mom's pissed," she said, sparing a glance at her home. "Might appear any sec. Let's get out of here." He shrugged, threw an arm around her shoulders, and dragged her onto the center of the road. "Gave you a hard time?" "She found out about the break-in." Ellis snickered. "Roger got it good too. Grounded for a month. Think his dad threw his computer out the window." "Serves him right. He's the one who gave us away." She lit the cigarette she had taken from the pouch, and offered her boyfriend one. He grunted appreciatively. "Sometimes, I don't even know why I bother," Michelle said quietly. "Going to school, trying to keep up appearances, all that crap. I'm just no good at studying. Can't solve a math problem to save my life. School's just hell for me." She looked at him gloomily. "Don't you wish the same thing?" Surprisingly, Ellis looked uncertain. "I dunno." "You don't know? Hell does that even mean?" "Getting into trouble is fun, don't get me wrong," he said hastily. "But..... I think we might regret this someday. My parents don't even give a shit anymore. After I graduate next year, they're gon na kick me out." "We can live together," she said, a tinge of hope in her voice. "I'll - I'll run away. With you." He looked at her incredulously. "We'll be eighteen. Eighteen, Mich. How the hell are we gon na afford rent? I don't even have any savings." "We'll think of something." "Of what? Work day to night at a Burger King? I hear even janitors need degrees these days to get a job. Don't you want to go to university?" For some reason, she was growing angrier with every word. "Maybe I haven't. Maybe all I've thought about is being with you. But now it seems you don't think the same." "Bae, I'm not - " "Stop lying to me! You don't give a shit about me. You're just like everyone else in my life. My stupid parents, my stupid teachers, all they have are expectations and more expectations. I can't believe you of all people - " "Grow up, Mich," Ellis roared. "A suspension isn't a small matter - " "Hey lovebirds!" They turned to see a man waving at them from a nearby field, a baseball mitt on one hand. "Sorry to interrupt, but you mind tossing that back to us?" Michelle followed his pointing finger to the ball at her feet. Slowly, she stooped to pick it up, rolling it in her hand and thinking. "Mind hurrying up?" the man called. She snarled and hurled it with all her might at the nearest parked car, shattering the side window utterly. An angry buzz rose from the players, while Ellis looked at her with jaw agape, but she ignored them all and stormed away. "Hell was that bitch thinking?" Floyd said, slapping a fist into his glove as he walked toward the car. The boy had run off after the girl, of course, leaving them to give an explanation when the owner showed up. Manny merely shrugged and said, "Kids these days." "Well, I'm not paying for - holy shit." A golden retriever poked its head out the window, panting heavily. Its coat shone with sweat as it dragged itself out of the car. As though exhausted by the ordeal, it collapsed onto the sidewalk, slobber pooling beneath its open mouth. "Shit, how long was it in there?" Manny said. "Hey boys, get some water over here!" Floyd shouted to his friends. Thanks for reading! I look down and I see nothing. Its like im a ghost. I want to feel something. Even if its not real, just to know that im alive. To know that I exist. I want to transverse worlds and travel oceans. I could have been a world class painter or maybe better yet a bullfighter in a rodeo. I want to feel alive. But no matter what I do, be it drugs or alcohol or sex, it, like most good things, never lasts. Its like if I wasn't here no one would have even been aware of my existence. Yet I exist still, for some reason or another. Sometimes I wish I could close my eyes and everything would just dissappear. But my thoughts pervade. I find it sad. Even in a lucid state I feel like im dreaming and that maybe one day things will happen that will snap me out of mt every day numbness. As the years pass I can feel my memories slowly fading. One day they will exist no more forever. Almost as if, I were imaginary.

My idea of a perfect evening was falling asleep in front of the TV with an empty bag of chips in my lap. I was kept up all night by the buzzing and stinging mosquitoes. After trying and failing miserably to pitch a tent, my full of herself cousin did it herself in a minute; People looked at me as if I was subhuman. Most of my family was composed of boy scouts and morning people who never stopped going on and on about the wonders of camping and how I should join them and that it was great for the soul. Whenever they went on a tangent, I would smile and nod, glancing at an exit all the while. It was September, but they had insisted that I come with them. This was the first time I had relented. All they'd given me was a smile that was too wide and a kit that was too big. I just wished the fan blew faster. - John was woken by hurried speaking and a tense atmosphere in the air. Confused, he looked out of his tent to see two of the senior camp counselors speaking in hushed voices while a bunch of teenagers in pajamas rubbed their eyes or looked around nervously. As he regained more of his senses, he was sure he could smell something thick in the air, like when he went to his dear mother who always put her pancakes on the stove a little bit too long, forcing him to politely refuse the blackened crust that might have once been batter. As his eyes adjusted to the moonlight, he realized that he was hot, too hot to be comfortable even though he was outside his tent with a mild breeze blowing, and then he saw the smoke stack that indicated a blazing inferno that was headed right for them. - " You there in the black shirt! Get everyone up and packing. " Zach said. Giving out orders, he felt like he was back at school on the field, hashing out plans with his team just before they went for the big match. He could feel a shadow of the adrenaline, his blood thumping as he was carried on his back, the cheers of the crowd reaching a crescendo. He ran his hand over his head before jamming it into his pockets. " Okay, what's the plan, big guy? " That voice, that slightly sarcastic tone that gave away the smirk beneath, he turned around to see Kelly, with none of the smirk he had come to associate her with. Looking at her, with her glasses that were always just a little crooked and her red hair in a mess, one could be forgiven for mistaking her as just a nerdy girl. Zach had experience dealing with all sorts of people, and in her green eyes he saw a look that he'd only seen on the crazy or the really angry guys on his team, the ones who took the game too seriously. When she'd gone against one of his best quarterbacks and come away with barely a scratch while the poor guy ended up in a hospital for harassing one of her lady friends, she'd earned his respect. Nodding, he took his hands out of his pockets, one of them coming out with a Smartphone. " I've called the fire department; the plan is to get as far away from that until the authorities arrive. " " That's stupid. You can't outrun fire " She said, snatching the phone from him. Mildly annoyed at his phone being taken, he said in the most cocky voice he could muster at this hour, " Well how would you know " She shot him a look, and for a brief second he felt like he had when he first applied at the team, making a wisecrack at the star player's expense. He'd looked like he'd gut him when the coach wasn't looking and leave him in a locker. He reminded himself he was a foot taller than her, but he still couldn't shake off the feeling that he'd nearly done something he would regret. She looked down at the phone. " I found out the hard way. It's how I lost Rover " There was a moment of awkward silence, with only the sound of flames flickering in the distance. During the long nights when both of them couldn't sleep they'd cuddle under the stars, a million times brighter than they were in the big city, recounting stories from their life. It was the only time he'd seen Kelly with her defenses truly down. She'd had the most beautiful smile on her face when she talked about her old dog and their adventures in the woods, about the times they'd play all sort of games, conversations where he couldn't speak but listened, understood. The times he'd saved her from drowning, and the time she'd saved him from the streets, taking him in. For the first and last time in the while he'd known her, she'd cried when said that she still wanted to play with him, and how she'd never hear his bark or hold him again. She'd been inconsolable, but he'd still tried. Contrary to what critics might say, he wasn't so dense that he'd ask her how it had happened. Ever since that day he thought he'd noticed something different about the way she walked, as if a great load had been lifted off of her, but he could never quite get his finger on it. " Um. Uh. Sorry. I'm so sorry I didn't kno- " She cut him off not with words, but with shoving the phone in his hands. Mercifully she didn't comment on his horrible apology, choosing to focus on the situation in hand while he swore at himself in the most colorful ways, certain that he'd cringe to this moment for years to come. " It's a map, I've marked a path through a nearby stream, and we should be safe on the other side. " " We'll never get there in time " " Not if we start now " - " Hey, Guys! huff wait up! " My body isn't designed for this Every morning, any observers would be alerted of my awakening by a groan and a shifting of position, where I would lay for another half hour before groaning again, louder this time. The bed was a trap. I'd stagger like a zombie into the bathroom, past my spotless toothbrush and straight to the shower. The shower was another trap. I'd stand there for a long time, with hot, cleansing water running down my body, sitting when I got too tired to stand. Sometimes I would think of life, death, the Universe, God, heaven and hell, the human endeavor, the meaning of life; War, disease, famine, technology. Other times, I would cup my hands trying to get as much water as I could into them so I could make a big splash. By the time my breakfast pizza had arrived and I'd gotten dressed, it was already afternoon. " Well, awful weather we're having " I heard a voice next to me where I was sure there was no one. I wasn't really surprised. My cousin had a habit of sneaking up on people, and in that he had no rival. He had light, silent footsteps, a thin inconspicuous frame and an eye for places where he might catch someone off guard. He fed off of attention, I didn't give him any. " Well, you look like you could use some help " He chuckled to himself, like it was the funniest thing in the world. He had an annoying habit of starting every sentence with " well ," and that got on my nerves. I gave him an annoyed look, " Well, if you're offering, now is as good a time as any " He smiled, and I anything that got even more on my nerves. Here we were, in a life and death scenario and all he could do was make light of it. I guess comedy really is a coping mechanism for some people. Whenever he smiled, I noticed this glint in his expression. Any teacher worth her salt would instantly identify him as a troublemaker, and they'd be right; Fred was the most infamous prankster in the county. He wasn't a bad kid, but he was a naughty one, the mischievous one. He lifted my too-heavy kit with deceptive strength for someone his size, and walked at twice the speed I had. " Well, see you on the other side! " I was soon left behind. Hiking through the woods, hearing the crackling of fire, inhaling the smoke and feeling the sweltering heat, anyone would be tired. By the time the stream was in sight, I was exhausted. All the others were already on the side while I trailed behind them. I was so relieved that I was finally going to be able to rest that my legs gave way before I allowed them to. I stumbled, and then fell face first into the mud. The knock to my head made my vision swim, making me lose further control of my body. I tried to stand, failing to find traction in the mud. The fire was dangerously close. It would be so nice to just lay there, sleep, and maybe take a little nap..... A was woken from the haze by screams. My own. The fire had reached me, and it was hungry. How was I supposed to fight against this, a force of nature, an element? It surrounded me, and I could hear words in the crackling, mocking me, judging me. Memories came flooding back, the sniggers, the bullying, the jokes, the contempt, the disappointment, and the failures. I coughed harder than all my previous bouts combined, my vision became flame and all I felt was pain. - " Any casualties " The paramedic who had come shortly after the fireman said. " Err, one. Smoke inhalation, second degree burns. Couldn't get clear of the fire fast enough " The paramedic nodded with a demeanor that suggested that he dealt with this every day. " Any first aid administered? " He said in a deep, clear voice. " We doused him with cold water..... " John replied. " Very good, we'll take it from here "

The hoard encroached on me, the numberless, shadow-covered husks shambling forth to claim me. I backed against the wall, staring at them. They came closer, and closer, and closer.
